passages.text: Detailed knowledge about the temporal and contextual dynamics of PAR signaling in VSMCs in vivo is currently lacking. There is therefore a need for a deeper understanding of the molecular switches that govern the transition from reparative to pathological PAR signaling in different phases of vascular injury and remodeling.
Insights from PAR deficient mouse models

The role of PARs in vivo was elucidated using PAR-deficient mouse models. PAR knockouts allowed to study early stages of development and only PAR1 absence showed a partial embryonic lethality. PAR2, PAR3 and PAR4 deficiency on the other hand showed no major developmental abnormalities until birth. However, PAR2 deficiency or resistance to proteolytic cleavage resulted in disturbed foetal haematopoiesis and partial perinatal lethality due to anaemia. While PAR-deficient mice were otherwise normal in postnatal development, induction of disease in PAR deficient mice revealed functional vascular roles of PAR.

Induction of arterial injury in PAR1-/- mice resulted in a higher VSMC density and impaired extracellular matrix formation during injury response. Furthermore, aortas from PAR1-/- mice failed to respond to induced endothelial dependent vasorelaxation. In angiotensin II induced hypertension, deficiency of PAR2 resulted in increased systolic arterial pressure and pulse pressure. In Ldlr-/- mice, the absence of PAR2 reduced atherosclerotic burden due to a decrease in CCL2- and CXCL1-induced monocyte infiltration. In mice on an ApoE-/- background, loss of PAR2 increased plaque stability and fibrous cap thickness, featuring decreased macrophage infiltration and decreased MMP-9 expression. Furthermore, atherosclerotic plaque burden of ApoE-/- PAR2-/- mice was reduced relative to ApoE knock-out alone with a concomitant decrease in lipid content and macrophage infiltration. Thus, loss of PAR2 attenuates atherosclerotic plaque formation in in vivo models.

PAR3 is expressed on mouse platelets along with PAR4. PAR3-/- mice showed an abnormal platelet response to thrombin stimulation. In addition, PAR4 deficiency caused prolonged bleeding times and in a model of arterial thrombosis induced by ferric chloride showed a protection from thrombosis. Absence of PAR4 also attenuated ischemia reperfusion injury in a model of middle cerebral artery occlusion.

Taken together, these studies suggest that PAR deficiency during the onset and progression of vascular diseases, such as atherosclerosis or aneurysm development, seems protective (Table 1). The role of PARs fit in the antagonistic pleiotropy hypothesis, in which proteins become redundant at later stages of life and even become detrimental. PARs could therefore have a detrimental role in adulthood, especially during cardiovascular disease, and might thus be a therapeutic target for intervention and treatment.

Vascular smooth muscle cell phenotype switching in vascular diseases

VSMCs are the main cell type in the medial layer of the vessel wall, maintain vessel tone, and allow vasoconstriction and vasodilatation. Under physiological conditions, VSMCs are in a contractile phenotype and abundantly express specific cytoskeleton and contractile proteins, resulting in a quiescent and non-proliferative state. VSMC contractile markers comprise calponin (CNN1), smooth muscle alpha-actin (alphaSMA), smooth muscle 22alpha (SM22alpha), and smooth muscle myosin heavy chain (SMMHC). Upon vessel injury, VSMCs have the plasticity to de-differentiate into a proliferative and migrative phenotype, synthesizing and secreting extracellular matrix (ECM) proteins, such as collagens and fibronectin, ensuring vessel wall repair. The fine tuning of this so-called phenotype switching is crucial to ensure a fast and effective vascular repair. However, upon continued stress VSMCs can enter pathological vascular remodelling and are involved in the development and progression of atherosclerosis, intimal hyperplasia, restenosis, aneurysm, vascular calcification, and vascular stiffness.
Phenotype switching of VSMCs

Phenotype switching of VSMCs is key in physiological and pathological arterial remodelling. Generally, the term "phenotypic switching" is utilized to denote the de-differentiation of VSMCs from a contractile to a synthetic state. However, this oversimplifies the de-differentiation of VSMCs as it can acquire multiple phenotypes (Table 2). The advent of techniques such as lineage tracing and single-cell sequencing has identified multiple VSMC types. Indeed, VSMCs can transdifferentiate to macrophage-like cells, fibroblast like cells, adipocyte-like cells, osteoblast/chondrocyte like cells, mesenchymal cells, and EC-like cells (Table 2).

Table 2 presents the different phenotypes VSMCs can acquire during phenotype switching. While the EC-like phenotype has been identified when VSMCs are subjected to laminar shear stress, the other VSMCs phenotypes have been characterized in atherosclerotic plaque analysis

Macrophage-like cells, resembling immune cells by expressing markers such as CD68 and Galectin-3, are involved in atherosclerotic plaque formation, engulfing lipids and initiating inflammation. Fibroblast-like cells express lumican (LUM), biglycan (BGN), decorin (DCN), and stem cell antigen 1 (Sca1), contribute to the formation of the fibrous cap producing collagen type I and fibronectin, stabilizing the plaque. Adipocyte-like cells expressing adipsin (CFD) and leptin (LEP) are implicated in lipid storage and metabolism within the plaque, influencing its composition. Osteoblast/chondrocyte-like cells express runt-related transcription factor 2 (RUNX2), SRY-related HMG-box (SOX9), osteocalcin (OCN), osteopontin (OPN), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and collagen (COL) I, II, X are responsible for the initiation and maturation of vascular calcification therefore affecting plaque stability. EC-like cells expressing CD31, CD144, and von Willebrand factor (VWF), participate in angiogenesis and neovascularization, which can contribute to plaque growth and vulnerability. During vascular remodelling and injury, medial VSMCs start de-differentiating by losing contractile markers (SM22alpha, CNN1, alphaSMA, SMMHC) and exhibiting a new set of cell-specific markers. The orchestrated transitions between these phenotypes highlight the dynamic nature of VSMCs during vascular remodelling, emphasizing their adaptive responses to the evolving arterial microenvironment.

Multiple factors have been identified that regulate phenotypic switching of VSMCs, suggesting an active process of de-differentiation rather than simply a loss of contractile markers. The list of molecular cues driving VSMC phenotype includes growth factors, transcriptional factors, cytokines, hormones, hemodynamic state, and components of the extracellular matrix, have all been extensively reviewed elsewhere. Next to these molecular and physical factors members of the blood coagulation cascade play a role in the regulation of VSMC phenotype. Indeed, coagulation proteases can either enter the vessel wall due to increased endothelial permeability or can be locally generated as observed in early and advanced vascular lesions. This led to the concept that slightly activated coagulation which does not result in thrombosis, can induce vascular remodelling. The next paragraph will report effects of blood coagulation proteases on PAR signalling related to VSMC phenotype.
Role of PARs signalling on vascular smooth muscle cell during vascular remodelling
EPCR/PAR1 signalling and vascular integrity

The endothelial protein C receptor (EPCR) is central for aPC generation and PAR1 mediated vascular protective mechanisms by the aPC. EPCR is a membrane-bound receptor that is expressed on the surface of ECs. The thrombin-thrombomodulin complex activates protein C and this reaction is facilitated when PC is bound to EPCR. aPC subsequently cleaves and inactivates FVa and FVIIIa, two procoagulant cofactors that are involved in the amplification of the clotting cascade. However, aPC also acts as a signalling molecule by activating PAR1 with EPCR serving as its co-receptor. Whereas thrombin cleaves PAR1 at Arginine 41 (R41), APC cleaves PAR1 at Arginine 46 (R46), resulting in differences in signalling. Tumour necrosis factor alpha (TNFalpha)-conditioned human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) treated with either thrombin or aPC showed a different pattern of gene expression, demonstrating that the same receptor can execute different functions. The beneficial effect of APC cleavage at R46 was demonstrated in vivo using mouse models with point mutations at either the R41 or R46 cleavage site of PAR1. Loss of PAR1 cleavage at R46, but not at R41 impaired hindlimb reperfusion and angiogenic sprouting.

Besides aPC and thrombin, other coagulation proteases have been identified to exert signalling via EPCR/PAR1. FXa requires binding to EPCR to activate PAR1 and to induce ERK1/2 activation, connective tissue growth factor (CTGF) expression and endothelial barrier protection. In addition, FVIIa binding to EPCR confers EC anti-inflammatory properties by signalling via PAR1 and beta-arrestin.

PAR1 biased signalling underscores the importance of directing PAR1 signalling towards attenuating proinflammatory activation and augmenting its anti-inflammatory pathways. The role of the EPCR has predominantly been investigated in ECs, however its expression and activity has been detected in VSMCs where it also serves as a cofactor for activation of PAR2 by FXa. In ECs, EPCR/PAR1 signalling has protective effects but its role in VSMCs is less clear.

In human atherosclerotic plaques, the fibrous cap consists of alphaSMA positive VSMCs expressing EPCR. This suggests that EPCR activation on VSMCs in the fibrous cap has a role in plaque development, progression and stability. Additionally, upregulation of VSMC EPCR is found in the neointima of rats following acute vascular injury. Further, platelet-derived growth factor BB (PDGF-BB) induces a synthetic VSMC phenotype, and significantly increases EPCR expression in a calcineurin/NFAT (nuclear factor of activated T cells) dependent manner. Taken together, the PAR1 co-receptor EPCR is associated with VSMC phenotype switching. However, our understanding of the role of EPCR in VSMCs is insufficient to conclude its involvement as protective or detrimental during plaque development.
PAR signalling in VSMCs during inflammation

Inflammation plays a critical role in vascular remodelling. During inflammation, immune cells are activated and release various cytokines that contribute to the remodelling process. IL-6, TNFalpha and interleukin 1-beta (IL-1beta) promote the recruitment of immune cells to the site of injury, and stimulate the production of MMPs that break down extracellular matrix proteins such as collagen and elastin. Low grade chronic or excessive inflammation contributes to pathological remodelling, including atherosclerosis and hypertension.

During inflammation and vascular injury, PDGF is released from activated platelets, macrophages, fibroblasts, VSMCs, and ECs. When PDGF-AB binds to its receptor on the surface of human cultured VSMCs it induces PAR1 gene expression. Increased PAR1 expression enhances the signalling effects of coagulation proteases, such as thrombin, which further amplifies the inflammation response. Indeed, in human VSMCs thrombin mediated PAR1 signalling increases inflammatory cytokines such as CCL11, interleukin 8 (IL-8), interleukin 6 (IL-6), IL-1beta, CXCL1, and macrophage chemoattractant protein 1 (MCP-1). Additionally, thrombin induced IL-1beta is dependent on PAR1 and NF-kappaB phosphorylation.

Reactive oxygen species (ROS) production is involved in the thrombin/PAR1 mediated release of proinflammatory cytokines by the p22phox-containing nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) oxidases (NOX1, NOX2 and NOX4). Thrombin-induced ROS production in murine VSMCs also involves Nox activator 1 (NoxA1) and the NADPH oxidase subunit p47phox. NADPH oxidases are responsible for the expression of tissue factor (TF) on the surface of VSMCs upon thrombin treatment via p38 MAPK, phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), and protein kinase B (Akt). TF complexes with FVIIa signal through PAR2, resulting in enhanced IL-8 and IL-6 expression. Taken together, thrombin increases ROS and inflammatory cytokine release in VSMCs and increases TF expression which further amplifies the proinflammatory and prothrombotic effects in the vessel wall (Fig. 2).
PARs during migration and proliferation

When a vessel wall injury occurs, VSMCs migrate to the site of injury and synthesize matrix thereby promoting the healing process. VSMCs are connected to the ECM via integrin-mediated adhesion (e.g. alpha5beta1 and alphavbeta3 ) with integrins acting as receptors for components of the ECM such as fibronectin, collagen, and laminin. Migration is initiated by various stimuli, such as growth factors, cytokines, and MMPs, which detach VSMCs from the underlying ECM. Thrombin-induced PAR activation has been shown to affect VSMC chemotaxis. Dronadula and colleagues showed that STAT3 phosphorylation, a mediator of cell growth and migration, together with cytosolic phospholipase A2 (PLA2) activation, is required to exert thrombin mediated VSMC motility. As previously mentioned, thrombin/PAR1 signalling drives ROS generation via NOX. In VSMCs, thrombin increases NOX-dependent ROS production which activates p38 MAPK leading to the expression of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), a VSMC chemoattractant. In line with this, mouse VSMCs deficient in NOX1 showed impaired migration after thrombin treatment.

Recent studies highlight galectin-3, a marker for macrophage-like VSMCs (Table 2), in thrombin-induced migration. Thrombin upregulates galectin-3, and its knockdown reduces ERK1/2 and p38 MAPK activation, impairing VSMCs migration. Galectin-3 elevated expression in heart disease makes it a potential biomarker for pathological remodelling. Additionally, thrombin induces endothelin-1 (ET-1) expression in retinal pigment epithelium via PAR1/RhoA. ET-1 is a vasoconstrictor and growth factor mainly synthesized by ECs that promotes migration of VSMCs from the media towards the intima. Whether thrombin induced ET-1 expression has a role in phenotype switching of VSMCs has yet to be elucidated.

Next to thrombin, FVIIa in complex with TF induces PAR2 signalling, transactivation of PDGF-Rbeta and stimulates migration of VSMCs. The role of TF-FVIIa-PAR2 complex in cell migration has mainly be investigated in cancer and metastasis, and a detailed mechanistic analysis on VSMCs is currently lacking.

After migrating to the site of injury, VSMCs synthesize extracellular matrix components, such as collagen to aid in the repair of the damaged vessel wall. However, excessive VSMC migration and proliferation can also contribute to cardiovascular disease (CVD), including atherosclerosis and restenosis. In here, VSMCs proliferate uncontrollably, leading to the formation of an unstable fibrous cap that can rupture. MMPs, such as MMP-2 and MMP-9, released from phenotypically switched VSMCs degrade ECM proteins further contributing to the destabilization of atherosclerotic plaques.

The increased proliferation of VSMCs is known to be modulated by thrombin. In rat VSMCs, the thrombin/PAR1-dependent cell growth occurs via activation of tyrosine kinases (JAKs) and STAT1/3. Moreover, thrombin stimulates VSMC proliferation through phosphorylation of the EGFR and ERK1/2. In this study, thrombin transactivated the EGFR, but proof that this transactivation is mediated via the cleavage of PAR1 is lacking. Thrombin induced VSMC proliferation is controlled by transcription factors such as Forkhead box-O (FoxO). Specifically, FoxO1 and FoxO3 are time dependently phosphorylated by PI3K. Inhibition of PI3K prevented VSMC proliferation induced by thrombin. Upstream of thrombin generation, FXa has been shown to activate both PAR1 and PAR2 inducing mitogenesis of VSMCs via RhoA signalling and the expression of sphingosine kinase-1 (S1P) and sphingosine-1-phosphate (SPHK1).

Graphic representation summarizing the main intracellular pathways after PAR activation in VSMCs. Thrombin/ PAR1 signalling has a major role in inducing cytokine release, migration, proliferation, and ROS production therefore further contributing to phenotypical changes in VSMCs. Illustration generated with BioRender.
PARs and extracellular vesicles

Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are nano-sized cell-derived structures released from the cellular membrane or the multivesicular body compartment of almost any cell and play an important role in cell-cell communication by carrying a range of nucleic acids and proteins. Due to their diverse and crucial roles in various physiological and pathological processes, EVs are gaining increasing interest and EVs have been associated with CVD risk. Subjects with moderate CVD risk display higher TF-dependent thrombin generation ex vivo and a higher number of circulating EVs is associated with a high 10-year CVD risk score. Thus, laboratory tests are now focusing on identifying the coagulation-inducing EVs by measuring the thrombin generation potential in in vitro assays. Yet, the question remains where these procoagulant EVs come from.

EVs are released in the circulation by multiple cell types, predominantly platelets, ECs and leukocytes. EVs are also released locally in the vessel wall by VSMCs. PDGF from activated platelets induces release of TF-positive EVs from synthetic VSMCs. TF-bearing EVs contribute to activation of the extrinsic coagulation pathway. Moreover, the activation of PAR2 via the TF-FVIIa-FXa complex induces the release of TF-positive EVs from ECs, whereas TF-FVIIa counteracts these pathways. It is not known if coagulation proteases similarly regulate the release of TF-positive EVs from VSMCs.

Procoagulant EVs can promote thrombin generation. Thrombin increases the release of EVs from VSMCs, which is prevented by Dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor. The activation of PAR1 and PAR3 by thrombin also increases the number of EV released and the protein cargo of mesenchymal stem cells via Rab5, early endosome antigen (EEA)-1, ERK1/2, and AKT. The ability of thrombin to induce EV release and change in protein content was also reported for platelets. Thrombin induces shedding of EVs with complex proteomic patterns rich in procoagulant and proadhesive proteins. These data suggest an important role of thrombin that goes beyond coagulation.

EVs not only carry proteins, but also nucleic acids such as RNA and DNA. Micro RNAs (miRNAs), which are small RNA molecules, regulate gene expression of target genes. By delivering miRNAs to recipient cells, EVs influence cellular processes such as proliferation, migration, and apoptosis. Increasing evidence shows that miRNAs carried by EVs can modulate atherosclerosis through regulating VSMC phenotype. EVs released from VSMCs are rich in the miRNA-143/145 cluster, influencing VSMC differentiation, phenotype switching, and vascular homeostasis. Interestingly, EVs derived from thrombin-stimulated platelets contain miRNA-223, miRNA-339 and miRNA-21 which are transferred to VSMCs and inhibit PDGFRbeta expression. In mouse models of atherothrombosis, PDGFRbeta is decreased in VSMCs within thrombotic areas. Since its agonist, PDGF-BB, is known to induce VSMC phenotype switching, inhibition of PDGFRbeta could therefore reduce phenotype switching. Further, EVs from activated platelets can induce a proinflammatory phenotype in VSMCs.

Overall, phenotype switching of VSMCs and subsequent PAR activation stimulates generation of procoagulant EVs. An increase in thrombin generation affects release and cargo of EVs responsible of further stimulating a synthetic VSMC phenotype.
PARs signalling in VSMC-EC crosstalk

Endothelial cells sense and respond to changes in fluid shear stress (FSS), translating these mechanical stimuli into biochemical signals. These signals profoundly influence VSMC behaviour by modulating pathways that intersect with PAR signaling. For instance, low FSS is known to induce TGF-beta release from ECs. TGF-beta activates Smad2/3 signalling in VSMCs promoting their transition to a synthetic VSMC phenotype. Further, also PAR2 activation in VSMCs triggers Smad2/3 signalling. In pancreatic cells, a direct interaction between TGF-beta receptor ALk5 and PAR2 has been shown by immunoprecipitation. Proof of ALK5 transactivating PAR2 is currently lacking in VSMCs but this interaction holds promise for therapeutic strategies to prevent maladaptive vascular remodelling.

ECs and VSMCs are mechanically coupled through vascular ECM and intercellular junctions, such as connexins. ECs upregulate MMPs, specifically MMP-1, in response to disturbed FSS. Additionally, MMP-1 can cleave PAR1 and trigger VSMC phenotype switching and arterial stenosis.

These findings underscore the complex interplay between EC-derived signals and PAR signaling in VSMCs, highlighting their synergistic contributions to Smad2/3 activation and VSMC phenotypic switching. Further research into PAR-mediated signaling in VSMCs-ECs crosstalk is needed.
Therapeutic approaches targeting PARs signalling
Vitamin K antagonists: effect of vitamin K-dependent coagulation proteases inhibition on the vasculature

Vitamin K antagonists (VKAs), such as warfarin, phenprocoumon and acenocoumarol, effectively reduce thromboembolic events by inhibiting the proper posttranslational modification and synthesis of vitamin K-dependent coagulation proteins. VKAs have been widely used for decades in clinical practise to treat a variety of thrombotic disorders, including atrial fibrillation, deep vein thrombosis, and mechanical heart valve replacement. While VKAs have been studied primarily for their anticoagulant activities, evidence suggests that VKAs may have direct effects on the vessel wall in addition to their antithrombotic action.

VKAs inhibits the enzyme vitamin K-epoxide reductase (VKORC1), and thereby the carboxylation of the four vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors: prothrombin, FVII, FIX, FX, and the anticoagulation factors protein C, protein S, and protein Z. VKAs also inhibits VKORC1L1, though to a lesser extent than VKORC1. While VKORC1 is essential for blood coagulation, the precise role of VKORC1L1 remains unclear. In coronary endothelial cells, VKORC1L1 has demonstrated anti-inflammatory effects, whereas suppression of VKORC1 enhances cell proliferation and viability.

With the discovery of vitamin K dependent proteins not involved in coagulation, VKAs have been shown to have off-target effects. VKAs reduces the carboxylation of vitamin K dependent matrix Gla protein (MGP) in cartilage and arteries. Like other Gla-containing proteins, MGP has a strong affinity for calcium ions which might explain its inhibitory role in vascular calcification. The carboxylated form of MGP has been detected in the apparently healthy arterial media, whereas the uncarboxylated form was located near calcified areas in atherosclerotic lesions. Because MGP plays an important role in calcification prevention, inhibiting its activity by warfarin can lead to increased atherosclerotic burden. Moreover, different cellular processes involved in the formation and progression of atherosclerotic plaques are affected by VKAs treatment, including oxidative stress, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, EV release therefore contributing to the VSMCs phenotype switching. Furthermore, VKAs also reduce circulating levels of aPC. It is known that aPC acts via EPCR/PAR1 signalling (see above) and elicits vascular protective effects by promoting endothelial barrier integrity. Therefore, a decrease in the protective a/EPCR/PAR1 signalling pathway might add to the list of detrimental effects of VKAs on the vasculature. Clinicians prescribing VKAs should remain mindful of the patient's arterial health, as it may be further compromised during VKAs therapy.

Although VKAs remain pivotal in the prevention and treatment of thromboembolic disease, their off-target effects on the vessel wall have spurred a shift toward the use of direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs).
Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs): effects of coagulation protease inhibition on vascular remodelling

DOACs are replacing traditional anticoagulants, such as VKAs, with its narrow therapeutic range, as the preferred choice due to their overall favourable safety profile (Table 3). Some common DOACs include the thrombin inhibitor Dabigatran-etexilate, and the direct FXa inhibitors, Rivaroxaban, Apixaban, and Edoxaban (Fig. 3). Further, interference with coagulation proteases activating PARs has emerged as potential therapeutic targets in various vascular diseases, atherosclerosis, and restenosis.

Role of coagulation proteases and PARs inhibition in vascular remodelling. During disease conditions such as atherosclerosis, aneurysm, or peripheral artery disease (PAD), vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) in remodelled vessels undergo phenotypic changes due to the activation of protease-activated receptors (PARs) by coagulation factors FXa and FIIa. Direct FXa inhibitors, including Rivaroxaban, Apixaban, and Edoxaban, together with heparins Fondaparinux and Enoxaparin, limit FXa/PAR2 signalling, thereby reducing VSMC migration and cytokine release. Dabigatran, a direct FIIa inhibitor, along with PAR1 inhibitors like Vorapaxar and Atopaxar, attenuate PAR1 signalling. This results in a decrease in cell proliferation, reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, extracellular vesicle (EV) release, migration, and cytokine release. Enoxaparin also has FIIa inhibiting activity, but to a lesser extent compared to its FXa inhibiting activity. Illustration generated with BioRender

The effect of Rivaroxaban on atherosclerosis has been extensively investigated. In ApoE-/- mice, Rivaroxaban treatment promotes plaque stability and decreased inflammatory cytokines IL-6, TNFalpha, and MCP-1. Furthermore, in ApoE-/- mice with pre-existing atherosclerotic plaques, Rivaroxaban mediated inhibition of FXa results in regression of advanced plaques. This effect could be explained by the reduced PAR2 signalling due to inhibition of FXa. Indeed, PAR1 and PAR2 expression in the atherosclerotic plaque was downregulated in Rivaroxaban treated mice compared to controls. This effect was attributed to reduced infiltration of macrophages in the plaque. Plaque regression could be explained by Rivaroxaban induced influences on macrophage polarization and subsequent decreased delta-like receptor 4 (Dll4), thereby inhibiting phenotype switching of VSMCs. Whether Rivaroxaban also promotes the contractile VSMC phenotype rather than only limiting the synthetic phenotype has still to be investigated.

Dabigatran-etexilate is a prodrug that is orally absorbed and in the liver converted to the active form Dabigatran by carboxylesterase. Dabigatran inhibits the action of thrombin, and it is prescribed to individuals with atrial fibrillation, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism (PE), or those who have undergone joint replacement surgery. Dabigatran has also been investigated in the context of atherosclerosis. In vitro, Dabigatran reduces levels of ROS and oxidative damage better than Rivaroxaban. These results were confirmed showing that Dabigatran reduced both thrombin induced ROS and EVs release from VSMCs in vitro. In vivo dabigatran reduced arterial thrombosis, lesion size, and increased plaque stability in ApoE-/- mice. Specifically, Dabigatran treatment inhibited the degradation of ECM, a process known to promote plaque vulnerability. However, further research is needed to fully understand the effects of DOACs on PAR signalling in VSMCs and subsequent vascular remodelling.
Heparin

Heparin is a class of naturally occurring polysaccharide that exhibit anticoagulant properties. Heparin binds to antithrombin (AT), a circulating serine protease inhibitor. When heparin binds to AT, it induces a conformational change that increases its activity by several hundredfold, thereby enhancing the inhibition of thrombin and FXa. Heparin is used as anticoagulant to prevent and treat hypercoagulability.

Commonly used heparins are Enoxaparin (FXa/thrombin inhibitor) and the synthetic Fondaparinux with increased selectivity as a FXa inhibitor (Fig. 3). With a carefully chosen dose to avoid unwanted bleeding, heparin was shown to inhibit aortic aneurysm and atherosclerosis development in angiotensin-II infused ApoE-/- mice. Specifically, inhibition of FXa and thrombin reduced PAR2-Smad2/3 signalling and downstream reduced MMP-2 expression, consequently limiting both aneurysm progression and atherosclerotic plaque development. Taken together, these data put forward the beneficial effects of limiting cellular responses triggered by PAR activation vascular remodelling.
Direct inhibition of PARs

Next to reducing the action of activated coagulation factors, PAR signalling can be inhibited by direct receptor-specific antagonists (Fig. 3). Vorapaxar, a direct PAR1 inhibitor, has been initially tested in combination with other antiplatelet drugs (aspirin and clopidogrel) in patients with acute coronary syndrome, and subsequently tested for secondary prevention in patients with a history of myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, and peripheral artery disease (PAD). Vorapaxar was associated with a significantly lower occurrence of MI or stroke. However, Vorapaxar led to significantly more intracranial bleeding than placebo, causing the study to be terminated early. This side effect may be related to the vascular protective effects of aPC/PAR1 signalling.

Upon thrombin stimulation, PAR1 dimerizes with PAR4 during platelet activation. PAR4 amplifies the high intracellular Ca2+ levels that support the late phase of platelet aggregation. The lack of a hirudin like domain in PAR4 makes it less sensitive to thrombin, therefore needing 10-fold higher thrombin concentrations to be activated. Thus, inhibition of PAR4 would still leave the thrombin/PAR1 signalling intact. Indeed, selective inhibition of PAR4, but not PAR1, significantly inhibits thrombin induced activation and fibrin deposition in human thrombi ex vivo. BMS-986,120 and BMS-986,141 are the only PAR4 antagonists that have entered clinical trials. BMS-986,120 was evaluated in a phase 1 dose finding study. Despite efficacy and a lack of adverse events no phase 2 studies of this compound followed. The first in-human-study testing BMS-986,141 on healthy individuals positively assessed the safety of BMS-986,141 and was published in February 2023. Since PAR4 is not only expressed by platelets but also VSMCs, studies investigating the inhibition of PAR4 and subsequent vascular remodelling should be taken in consideration.

Pepducins are another category of direct PARs inhibitors. They are highly selective lipidated peptides that target the intracellular loops of PAR receptors blocking the receptor-G-protein interface. The PAR1 inhibitor PZ-128 (P1pal-7) successfully completed phase 2 clinical trials. In combination with standard antiplatelet therapy PZ-128 was shown to be safe and reduced adverse outcomes in patients undergoing cardiac catheterization. Whether PZ-128 has direct effects on VSMCs has not being investigated yet. However, a PAR1 agonist pepducin (P1pal-13) was tested in mouse VSMCs. The study found that P1pal-13 significantly stimulates the proliferation and hyperplasia of VSMCs in the carotid artery following injury. P1pal-13 activates both PAR1 and PAR1-PAR2 complexes, leading to marked increases in medial and intimal hyperplasia, ultimately resulting in arterial stenosis. Interestingly, this hyperplastic response was absent in PAR1- or PAR2-deficient mice, indicating that both receptors are required for the proliferative effects.

In mice, the PAR2 inhibitor PZ-235 attenuated the initiation and the progression of abdominal aortic aneurysm with reduced plasma levels of IL1-beta, MCP-1 and MMP-2. Additionally, PZ-235 demonstrated significant protection against liver fibrosis, necrosis and inflammation in an experimental mouse model of.

Non-alcoholic Steatohepatitis (NASH). Oasis Pharmaceuticals is conducting evaluations of PZ-235, including its analogues OA-235i and OA-235c, for treating conditions like non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), kidney fibrosis, and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). Phase 1 clinical trials are underway with the PAR2 inhibitor OA-235i in NASH patients.

Systemic effects and translational challenges of targeting PARs

PARs are widely expressed in various tissues, including the vasculature, nervous system, and epithelial barriers. In here, PARs mediate diverse physiological processes such as coagulation, inflammation, tissue repair, pain perception, and vascular tone regulation. The systemic effects of targeting PAR signaling stem from their central role in maintaining homeostasis. For instance, PAR1, activated by thrombin, is crucial for platelet aggregation and endothelial barrier integrity. Therapeutic inhibition of PAR1 may effectively prevent thrombosis but can also impair vascular repair, increase bleeding risk, and disrupt endothelial integrity, leading to vascular leakage. Similarly, PAR2 is involved in inflammatory and pain responses, and holds promise as a target in inflammatory bowel disease or arthritis. However, systemic inhibition of PAR2 may compromise host defence mechanisms by reducing epithelial repair capacity and altering immune cell recruitment at mucosal surfaces.

An additional consideration is the capacity of PARs to heterodimerize, which can enhance downstream signaling. For instance, PAR1-PAR2 heterodimerization has been implicated in sepsis, while PAR1-PAR4 heterodimerization plays a role in arterial thrombosis. These findings highlight the limitations of therapies targeting a single PAR, as such an approach may not achieve comprehensive therapeutic efficacy. To address this challenge, dual receptor inhibition has emerged as a promising strategy. Notably, a bivalent antagonist targeting both PAR1 and PAR2 has been developed, demonstrating efficacy in inhibiting intracellular calcium mobilization.

Moreover, the ability of PARs to transactivate other receptor types including receptor-serine/threonine- kinase (RSTK), receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), toll-like receptors (TLRs), and NOD-like receptors (NLRs) markedly increases the possible off target effects of PAR inhibition.

The systemic effects of targeting PARs pose significant translational challenges. Specificity is difficult to achieve due to the structural similarity of PAR family members and their shared signaling pathways. Off-target effects, such as interfering with the coagulation cascade or epithelial barrier function, could lead to adverse events, limiting the clinical utility of PAR-targeted therapies. Further, species-specific differences in PARs expression and function are observed in mouse and human platelets. As a result, bridging laboratory findings to clinical practice will necessitate a greater emphasis on human studies.

Additionally, the lack of biomarkers to measure PAR activation in vivo complicates patient stratification and therapeutic monitoring. Addressing these challenges requires innovative approaches, such as localized drug delivery systems, selective allosteric modulators, or transient inhibitors that modulate PAR activity without causing prolonged systemic disruption. Future research into the tissue-specific roles of PARs and their interaction networks will be critical to mitigate risks and maximize the therapeutic potential of these targets.
Future perspectives

PARs play a critical role in VSMC signaling and hold significant implications for CVD research and therapy. Future studies on PAR signaling in VSMCs could greatly benefit from the application of advanced technologies and interdisciplinary approaches. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) offers the potential to unravel the heterogeneity of VSMCs and elucidate context-specific PAR signaling pathways within distinct subpopulations, especially in pathological vascular remodelling. Similarly, advanced imaging techniques, such as super-resolution microscopy and intravital imaging, can provide real-time visualization of PAR activation and its downstream effects at subcellular resolution, shedding light on spatial and temporal dynamics. Integrative bioinformatic tools are valuable for integrating multi-omics data, enabling the identification of novel regulatory networks and therapeutic targets within the PAR signaling axis. The identification of reliable biomarkers for PAR activation, such as phosphorylated substrates, effector proteins, or EV-derived microRNAs, could enhance our ability to monitor disease progression and therapeutic efficacy non-invasively. Liquid biopsy technologies, which detect these biomarkers in blood samples, hold promise in this regard.

However, significant challenges remain in developing PAR antagonists or inhibitors specifically targeting VSMCs. A major limitation arises from the dual role of PAR signaling in both vascular remodelling and coagulation (see above).
Conclusions

Our review underscores the complex role of PAR mediated signalling during pathological vessel wall remodelling and emphasizes the need for further research into the molecular mechanisms and downstream signalling pathways of PAR activation. Such investigations will not only deepen our understanding of PAR signalling in VSMCs but also advance the development of safer, more effective treatments for cardiovascular disease.

passages.text: Diversifying T-cell responses: safeguarding against pandemic influenza with mosaic nucleoprotein
ABSTRACT

Pre-existing T-cell responses have been linked to reduced disease severity and better clinical outcomes during the 2009 influenza pandemic and the recent COVID-19 pandemic. We hypothesized that diversifying T-cell responses, particularly targeting conserved viral proteins such as the influenza A virus (IAV) nucleoprotein (NP), could protect against both epidemic and pandemic IAV strains. To test this, we created a mosaic nucleoprotein (MNP) by synthesizing a sequence that maximized the representation of 9-mer epitopes from 7422 NP sequences across human, swine, and avian IAVs. Notably, the MNP sequence showed high homology with the NP of the H5N1 strain affecting dairy cows in the ongoing outbreak. Mucosal immunization with the adjuvanted MNP vaccine induced robust CD8 and CD4 T-cell responses against both known immunodominant and in silico predicted subdominant epitopes. MNP-vaccinated mice challenged with epidemic H1N1 and H3N2 strains, which shared immunodominant CD8 and/or CD4 T-cell epitopes, showed a significant (~4 log) reduction in lung viral load. Importantly, MNP-vaccinated mice challenged with a pandemic H1N1 strain lacking shared immunodominant CD8 or CD4 epitopes exhibited a superior reduction in lung viral load, linked to T-cell responses targeting subdominant epitopes present in both the MNP and pandemic strain NP. These results suggest that a diversified T-cell response induced by the MNP vaccine could provide broad protection against severe disease from both current and emerging IAV strains.
IMPORTANCE

The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that seasonal influenza causes 3-5 million cases of severe illness annually. The influenza virus frequently undergoes genetic changes through antigenic drift and antigenic shift, resulting in annual epidemics and occasional pandemics. Consequently, a major public health objective is to develop a universal influenza vaccine that offers broad protection against both current and pandemic influenza A strains. In this study, we designed a nucleoprotein (NP) antigen (termed mosaic NP) comprising antigenic regions found in thousands of influenza viruses, aiming to use it as a vaccine to induce broad anti-influenza T-cell responses. Our findings indicate that the mosaic NP vaccine provided significant protection against seasonal H1N1 and H3N2, as well as the pandemic H1N1 strain, demonstrating its effectiveness across various influenza subtypes. These findings suggest that the mosaic NP is a potential universal influenza vaccine antigen, capable of protecting against diverse strains of influenza viruses.
INTRODUCTION

The influenza virus presents a significant global health threat, with mutations in its hemagglutinin surface glycoprotein leading to antigenic drifts and the continual generation of new variants, precipitating annual influenza epidemics worldwide. Current antibody-based vaccines primarily target the variable hemagglutinin (HA) surface glycoprotein, but they exhibit reduced effectiveness against antigenically distinct drifted subtypes of influenza A viruses (IAVs), highlighting the need for alternative approaches. Notably, T-cell responses, particularly those targeting internal proteins, demonstrate broad reactivity across various IAV subtypes. Evidence suggests that pre-existing cross-reactive T-cell responses were protective against severe disease during the 2009 swine influenza pandemic and also expedited recovery in individuals infected with H7N9 and other IAV strains. This has sparked considerable interest in harnessing T-cell immunity to develop universal vaccines capable of providing cross-protection against diverse influenza strains, representing a promising avenue in the ongoing battle against the virus.

There are multiple approaches to the design of broadly reactive vaccines to address the challenge of pathogen diversity. One is to focus on conserved antigens, those parts of the pathogen least likely to mutate over time, such as influenza nucleoprotein (NP). Another approach is to formulate multivalent vaccines that include several variants of the same protein, such as the trivalent influenza vaccine. Both approaches still fall short of capturing maximum epitope diversity, and therefore another strategy is to specifically aim for centralized antigens, either by phylogenetic identification of an evolutionally central strain or by algorithmically averaging, where sequences from multiple variants of the same protein are combined into a single synthetic construct, typically as a consensus sequence. Mosaic protein sequences are an alternative approach to consensus sequence design and are crafted through a computational process that incorporates epitopes from diverse viral strains, into a single synthetic antigen. This contrasts with consensus sequences, which are constructed by averaging sequences across variants to form a generalized, representative profile. Mosaic proteins are designed using algorithms that optimize epitope coverage to ensure broad reactivity against multiple IAV strains. Such methodologies aim to maintain epitopes that are both common and rare across strains, maximizing the immune system's ability to recognize different viruses. Prior studies have demonstrated the superiority of mosaic over consensus sequence approaches in vaccine design, particularly in their capacity to elicit a wider breadth of immune responses. This was notably demonstrated in the field of HIV vaccines, where mosaic antigens provided superior coverage against global HIV isolates compared to consensus designs. The broad protective potential of mosaic-based vaccines has also been validated in influenza research. Prior work has shown that mosaic hemagglutinin constructs conferred protection against a wide spectrum of influenza subtypes in various species, reflecting a significant advance toward a universal influenza vaccine. This included effective protection in mice, chickens, and monkeys against both seasonal and highly pathogenic avian influenza strains. Considering the highly conserved nature of the nucleoprotein (NP) in influenza viruses, the application of mosaic technology to NP could be particularly advantageous.

In this study, we designed mosaic NP (MNP) based on all available sequences derived from human, avian, and swine IAV strains. The resulting MNP was tested for T-cell-mediated viral control when administered with vaccine adjuvants known to induce robust T-cell immune responses. Compared to the recombinant NP (PR8-NP) derived from the H1N1 Influenza A/PR/8/34 (IAV-PR8) strain, the MNP elicited CD4 T-cell responses against a broader pool of epitopes in mice and demonstrated superior protective efficacy against pandemic IAV, as compared to PR8 NP.
RESULTS
Characterization of mosaic NP

We designed a single influenza virus nucleoprotein (termed mosaic NP, consisting of amino acids that are naturally present in the influenza virus nucleoproteins from different viral strains), which incorporates the maximum number of 9-mer sequences derived from 7422 NP sequences in the database (designed using the Mosaic Vaccine tool available at hiv.lanl.gov.). The resulting 498-amino-acid (AA) MNP was then analyzed for its coverage across all possible 9-mer epitopes found in the entire set of 7422 NP sequences. Remarkably, greater than 77% of all possible NP 9-mers were covered by the MNP (Fig. S1A). Coverage of all epitopes was nearly complete when 9-mer epitopes are only off by 2 (Table 1) or fewer amino acids; 2 AA mismatched coverage of all NP 9-mer epitopes by MNP was greater than for sample natural sequences. While the MNP sequence was designed for optimal 9-mer coverage, we additionally evaluated for 12-mer and 14-mer coverage attained against natural NP sequences and found that the exact coverage of unique epitopes within the pool of 7422 sequences was approximately 19%-27% higher, as compared to the natural NP sequences of epidemic and pandemic IAV strains (Table 1).

passages.text: To demonstrate the capacity of the MNP to capture sequence diversity among both avian and mammalian influenza NP genes, we generated a network graph (Fig. 1A) that visualizes the degree of 9-mer overlap between representative influenza sequences. Avian sequences form a densely connected cluster, distinctly separate from a more dispersed group of mammalian sequences. The synthetic Mosaic NP sequence is centrally located between these clusters, exhibiting extensive shared NP 9-mer overlaps with both avian and mammalian sequences, as evidenced by numerous connecting edges, and high average 9-mer overlap. Furthermore, AA sequence comparison between the MNP and the six representative IAV strains including the recent bovine epidemic H5N1 strain (two of H1N1, two of H3N2, and two of H5N1) resulted in the consensus AA sequences of NP and there were only five amino acid differences between the generated consensus sequence and the MNP (Fig. S1B). It is noteworthy that the MNP exhibited the highest similarity with the newly reported highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 strain that infected cattle in 2024, which was not present in the database used for the generation of MNP (Fig. 1B). The recombinant protein generated from this MNP sequence was successfully expressed in BL21 (DE3) E. coli and purified using Ni-NTA affinity chromatography (Fig. 1C and D).

Characterization and synthesis of mosaic NP. (A) Influenza sequences were identified by extracting unique 9-mers from the mosaic-derived 7422 NP amino acid sequences and calculating Jaccard similarities between the sequences to assess shared motifs. A network graph was constructed, where nodes represent NP sequences and edges indicate significant 9-mer overlap. Mammalian and avian hosts were differentiated by distinct node shapes, and the Mosaic NP, and reference sequences were highlighted. The average shared 9-mer overlap is indicated by node colors. (B) The phylogenetic distance between the aligned sequences was calculated and visualized using the neighbor-joining method based on the BLOSUM62 scoring. (C) SDS-PAGE analysis of mosaic protein expression in sonicated E. coli cells following induction at either 16 C or 37 C. Lane M: protein marker. Lanes 1 and 2: supernatant and pellet from 16 C induction, respectively. Lanes 3 and 4: supernatant and pellet from 37 C induction, respectively. (D) SDS-PAGE analysis of HIS-tag purification from supernatants of sonicated cells induced at 37 C induced. Lane M: protein marker. Lane 1: flow through. Lane 2: elution.
Mosaic nucleoprotein elicits potent T-cell responses and protects against lethal challenge with H1N1 influenza A virus

To assess whether MNP is immunogenic, we formulated the protein in a combination adjuvant consisting of Adjuplex (ADJ; carbomer-based adjuvant) and glucopyranosyl lipid A (GLA; TLR-4 agonist), as described previously. For rigor, the PR8 NP from the IAV-PR8 strain was included as a positive control, and mice were vaccinated twice intranasally, at an interval of 3 weeks. It is noteworthy that the immunodominant Db-restricted NP366 and I-Ab-restricted NP311 epitopes in the PR8 NP are conserved in the MNP (Fig. 2A). On the 8th day after vaccination, we quantified NP366- and NP311-specific T-cell responses in lungs. In the lungs of vaccinated mice, approximately 10% of lung tissue CD8 T cells were specific to NP366 epitope, and ~2% of CD4 T cells were specific to the NP311-epitope (Fig. 2B). The percentages of NP366- or NP311-specific T cells in lungs of PR8 NP and MNP groups were similar, which suggested that the MNP is as immunogenic as the native PR8 NP protein for these immune dominant epitopes.

Mosaic and PR8 NP vaccine-induced reduction in homologous Influenza A viral titers in lungs. Cohorts of 7- to 12-week-old mice were vaccinated intranasally twice with either mosaic NP (MNP) or PR8 NP formulated in ADJ + GLA. (A) Sequence comparisons between the PR8 NP and the MNP were performed for the regions NP311-325 and NP366-374, which are immunodominant epitopes for the PR8 NP. (B) By staining with MHC I or MHC II tetramers, NP311- and NP366-specific CD4 and CD8 T cells were quantified at 8 days after booster vaccination. (C-E) At 120 days after booster vaccination, mice were challenged with the IAV-PR8 virus. (C) Six days after the challenge, viral titer was quantified in the lungs and weight loss was monitored. (D) Using MHC tetramers, NP311- and NP366-specific CD4 and CD8 T cells were quantified in the lungs on the 6th day after the challenge. (E) Lung NP366- and NP311-specific T cells producing IFN-gamma were quantified by ex vivo stimulation with the respective peptides. Planned pairwise group comparisons were conducted using Welch's ANOVA followed by Welch's t-tests, or an unpaired t test for two-group comparisons. *, **, ***, and **** denote significance at P < 0.05, 0.01, 0.001, and 0.0001, respectively. "ns" indicates results that are "not significant." The data in each graph represent the mean +- SEM. Data are representative of at least two independent experiments. The FACS plots generated from concatenated data from all mice in the respective group show the percentages of cells within the gate among CD8 or CD4 T cells, which correspond to the average values across individual samples.

Since MNP elicited immunodominant epitope-specific effector CD4 and CD8 T cells at levels comparable to that of PR8 NP, we assessed viral protection by challenging vaccinated and unvaccinated mice with the pathogenic IAV-PR8 strain. At 120 days after vaccination, mice were challenged intranasally with a lethal dose of IAV-PR8. Remarkably, the lungs of mice vaccinated with the PR8 NP or the MNP contained approximately 4 logs lower viral titers, as compared to lungs from unvaccinated mice. Consistent with accelerated virus control, recovery from weight loss in vaccinated mice started from the 4th day after the viral challenge (Fig. 2C). Next, we examined whether viral control in the lungs of MNP-vaccinated mice was linked to strong recall responses of vaccine-induced memory T cells. On the 6th day after viral challenge, we detected high percentages of NP366-specific CD8 T cells and NP311-specific CD4 T cells in lungs of both PR8 NP- and MNP-vaccinated mice (Fig. 2D). Furthermore, NP366-specific CD8 T cells and NP311-specific CD4 T cells readily produced IFN-gamma, upon ex vivo antigenic stimulation (Fig. 2E). Taken together, data in Fig. 2 strongly suggested that (i) MNP is appropriately processed by the antigen presentation machinery to elicit NP366-specific and NP 311-specific effector and memory T cells; (ii) memory T cells induced by MNP are appropriately programmed for swift recall responses and effectively reduce influenza viral load in lungs; and (iii) conserved immunodominant epitopes are sufficient for T-cell-dependent viral control to IAV.
T-cell responses to conserved immunodominant epitopes in the mosaic nucleoprotein protect against the H3N2 influenza A virus

Data in Fig. 2 showed that mosaic NP formulated in ADJ + GLA elicited T-cell memory to immunodominant epitopes and protected against the H1N1 influenza A virus. Next, we compared the amino acid sequence of MNP with the NP of the H3N2 Influenza A/Aichi/2/1968 strain (IAV-Aichi). While the MHC II-restricted NP311 epitope in the MNP and IAV-Aichi NP are identical, the MHC I-restricted NP366 epitope of IAV-Aichi differs from the MNP epitope in two amino acids at positions 7 and 8 of the sequence (Fig. 3A). To assess whether the two amino acid difference in the NP366 epitope in the IAV-Aichi virus was sufficient to evade T-cell immunity induced by the MNP, cross-reactivity between the two epitopes was measured after vaccination, and viral titers were assessed following the challenge. We vaccinated cohorts of mice with PR8 NP or the MNP. Eight days after vaccination, lung T cells were stimulated with the Aichi-NP366 ASNENMDAM peptide, and cytokine expression, including IFN-gamma and IL-17a, was measured (Fig. 3B). Results showed that PR8- or MNP-induced NP366-specific CD8 T cells were responsive to NP366-Aichi peptide stimulation, but the percentages of responding cells were lower, as compared to the percentages of cells that responded to the NP366-PR8 peptide. Six months after vaccination, we challenged vaccinated and unvaccinated mice with IAV-Aichi, and lung viral titers were quantified on the 6th day after the challenge. Results showed sustained weight loss in all three groups, but both vaccinated groups exhibited significant reductions in viral titers, as compared to the unvaccinated control group (Fig. 3C). We determined whether lower lung viral burden in vaccinated groups was associated with robust recall CD8 and/or CD4 T-cell responses. Mismatch of two amino acid residues in the NP366 epitope between the IAV-Aichi NP and the MNP or PR8 NP led to substantive variability in the magnitude of the NP366-specific recall CD8 T-cell responses in lungs of vaccinated mice (Fig. 3D and E). These results, along with the data on the lower T-cell response to the vaccine (Fig. 3B), suggested incomplete cross-reactivity, which may also explain the relatively higher lung IAV-Aichi viral titers, as compared to the lungs of MNP-vaccinated mice following PR8 challenge. However, consistent with the conservation of the NP311 epitope in PR8 NP, MNP, and the IAV-Aichi NP, NP311-specific recall CD4 T-cell responses were less variable and uniformly strong in both vaccinated groups (Fig. 3D and E). In response to ex vivo stimulation with the respective peptides, lung NP366- and NP311-specific T cells produced IFN-gamma and/or IL-17. Thus, despite high variability in the NP366-specific response, strong and consistent CD4 T-cell response was sufficient to achieve effective viral control in the lungs of MNP-vaccinated mice.

Cohorts of 7- to 12-week-old mice were vaccinated intranasally twice with either MNP or PR8 NP formulated in the combination adjuvant ADJ + GLA. At 6 months after booster vaccination, mice were challenged with the H3N2 Influenza A/Aichi/2/1968 strain; unvaccinated mice were challenged as controls. (A) Sequence comparisons were performed between PR8 NP, MNP, and Aichi NP for the two immunodominant epitopes NP311-325 and NP366-374. (B) Lung CD8 T cells producing IFN-gamma and/or IL-17 were quantified by ex vivo stimulation with the Aichi-NP366 or the PR8 NP366 peptide on day eight after booster vaccination. (C) Six days after the challenge, viral titer was quantified in the lungs and weight loss was monitored. (D) Using MHC tetramers, NP311- and NP366-specific CD4 and CD8 T cells were quantified in the lungs on the 6th day after the challenge. (E) Lung NP366- and NP311-specific T cells producing IFN-gamma and/or IL-17 were quantified by ex vivo stimulation with the respective peptides. Planned pairwise group comparisons were conducted using a one-way ordinary ANOVA followed by Fisher's least-significant difference (LSD) test, or an unpaired t test was used for two-group comparisons. *, **, ***, and **** denote significance at P < 0.05, 0.01, 0.001, and 0.0001, respectively. "ns" indicates results that are "not significant." The data in each graph represent the mean +- SEM. The FACS plots generated from concatenated data from all mice in the respective group show the percentages of cells within the gate among CD8 or CD4 T cells, which correspond to the average values across individual samples.
Heterosubtypic T-cell immunity to pandemic IAV H1N1-2009 strain

The presence of pre-existing T-cell responses has been associated with less severe influenza disease in humans during the H1N1 pandemic of 2009 and improved recovery following H7N9 infections. Here, we investigated whether the collection of epitopes in the MNP can protect against the pandemic Influenza A/California/04/2009 (IAV-CA04) strain. Mice were vaccinated with the MNP or the H1N1 PR8 NP and challenged with the IAV-CA04 virus at 6 weeks after vaccination. While control mice displayed continuous weight loss following the viral challenge, mice vaccinated with PR8 NP, or the MNP showed recovery beginning on day 4 after the viral challenge (Fig. 4A). The lungs from both PR8 NP and MNP mice contained lower viral burden, as compared to controls. Notably, viral load in the lungs of mice vaccinated with MNP was significantly lower (P < 0.05) than in the lungs of PR8 NP mice (Fig. 4A). MNP-vaccinated mice showed enhanced viral control when challenged with IAV-CA04 even 5 months after vaccination (Fig. 4B). Thus, the collection of T-cell epitopes in the MNP provided enhanced protection against the pandemic strain of IAV.

Mosaic and PR8 NP vaccine-induced reduction in pandemic H1N1 influenza A virus titers in the lungs. Cohorts of 7- to 12-week-old mice were vaccinated intranasally twice with either MNP or PR8 NP formulated in the combination adjuvant ADJ + GLA. At 6 weeks or 5 months after booster vaccination, mice were challenged with the H1N1 Influenza A/California/04/2009 strain. Mice that were given only adjuvant were used as controls for the challenge. (A) Percent weight loss and viral titer in the lungs were assessed on the 6th day after the challenge in mice at 6 weeks post-booster vaccination. (B) Percent weight loss and viral titer in the lungs were assessed on the 6th day after the challenge in mice at 5 months post-booster vaccination. (C) By staining with MHC tetramers NP311- and NP366-specific CD4 and CD8 T cells were quantified in the lungs on the 6th day after the challenge. (D) Sequence comparisons were conducted among PR8 NP, MNP, and CA04 NP for the NP311-325 and NP366-374 regions. (E) At day 6 after viral challenge, lung NP366- and NP311-specific T cells producing IFN-gamma, IL-2, TNF-alpha, and/or IL-17 were quantified by ex vivo stimulation with the respective peptides. (F) Lung CD8 and CD4 T cells producing IFN-gamma and/or IL-17 were quantified by ex vivo stimulation with the CA04-NP366 or CA04-NP311 peptide, respectively, on day 8 after booster vaccination. Planned pairwise group comparisons were made using either ordinary one-way or two-way ANOVA with multiple comparisons using Fisher's LSD test. *, **, ***, and **** denote significance at P < 0.05, 0.01, 0.001, and 0.0001, respectively. "ns" indicates results that are "not significant." The data in each graph represent the mean +- SEM. Data are from three independent experiments.

To understand the immunological basis for the protection afforded by the PR8 NP and MNP and the differences in the degree of protection induced by MNP and PR8 NP vaccinations, we quantified CD8 and CD4 T-cell responses to the immunodominant epitopes NP366 and NP311, respectively. Surprisingly, despite a >90% reduction in viral load, NP366-specific CD8 T cells and NP311-specific CD4 T cells in the lungs of IAV-CA04-challenged mice showed no evidence of recall expansion (Fig. 4C), unlike the robust recall T-cell responses following challenge with PR8 and IAV-Aichi viruses (Fig. 2 and 3).

To understand the lack of recall responses to immunodominant epitopes following viral challenge, we compared amino acid sequences for the NP366 and NP311 epitopes in the PR8 NP, MNP, and the IAV-CA04 virus NP. While the NP366 epitope is identical in IAV PR8 NP and the MNP, the NP366 epitope of CA04 contained a single substitution at the sixth amino acid (methionine [M] to valine [V] substitution) (Fig. 4D), which is known to be sufficient to abrogate recognition by CD8 T cells that are specific to the Db/NP366 complex. After the challenge of PR8 or MNP-vaccinated mice with IAV-CA04, neither the PR8- and MNP-derived NP366 peptides nor the CA04-derived NP366 peptide induced cytokine expression in lung CD8 T cells (Fig. 4E). Moreover, 8 days post-MNP vaccination, lung T cells showed minimal cytokine production by CD8 T cells upon stimulation with the NP366-CA04 peptide (Fig. 4F). Thus, the lack of recall expansion of vaccine-induced memory NP366-specific CD8 T cells can be explained by the loss of their reactivity to the NP366 epitope of the IAV-CA04 virus. For the MHC II-restricted NP 311-325 epitope, the tyrosine (Y; at the third position) and isoleucine (I; at the sixth position) were substituted with valine (V) and methionine (M), respectively (Fig. 4D). Like what was observed for CD8 T cells, NP311-specific CD4 T cells induced by the PR8 or MNP vaccine did not exhibit cross-reactivity to stimulation with the NP311-CA04 peptide (Fig. 4E and F). Thus, the amino acid substitutions at the third and sixth residues of the NP311 epitope in the CA04 NP were sufficient to abrogate recognition by vaccine-elicited NP311-specific memory CD4 T cells. In summary, amino acid substitutions in the immunodominant epitopes of the CA04 NP likely abolished the ability of pre-existing vaccine-induced immunodominant epitope-specific memory T cells to recognize and respond to CA04 challenge.
Broader reactivity of CD4 T cells elicited by mosaic NP is associated with enhanced control of pandemic influenza virus

Because vaccine-induced immunity to IAV-CA04 cannot be explained by recall responses to immunodominant epitopes NP366 and NP311, we hypothesized that T-cell responses to other epitopes in the MNP mediate viral control in the lungs. Therefore, we conducted epitope prediction restricted to mouse MHC Class I and II for CA04, PR8, and MNP and compared the predicted amino acid sequences among the three proteins. The top 10 predicted regions are summarized in Tables 2 and 3. The CD8 T-cell epitope prediction identified that the top six epitope sequences covered the same region across CA04 NP, PR8 NP, and MNP. However, as observed for NP366 in CA04 NP, not all the predicted epitope sequences were identical across NP proteins. It is noteworthy that, the MNP design incorporated the maximum number of possible MHC I-restricted 9-mer epitopes. Here, we assessed whether such a 9-mer-based design altered MHC II-restricted CD4 T-cell epitopes in the MNP. As expected, the historical epitope in the NP311 region was predicted for PR8 NP and MNP, but not for the CA04 NP. However, highly ranked epitopes were predicted in the three regions spanning amino acids 417-431, 263-277, and 75-89 of the CA04 NP, and among the three, regions 263-277 and 75-89 were also predicted for PR8 NP and MNP (Fig. 5A). Interestingly, the 417-431 region was predicted for MNP and CA04 NP, but not PR8 NP. Next, to validate the in-silico epitope prediction, we examined the antigenic reactivity of lung T cells from vaccinated mice challenged with IAV-CA04 by stimulating with IAV-CA04 NP peptide pools composed of 14-16 amino acids or synthetic peptides derived from the top 10 predicted CD8 T-cell epitopes listed in Table 2 (Fig. S2). None of the peptides stimulated CD8 T cells to produce IFN-gamma or IL-17a at levels above the media control, indicating a lack of notable recall expansion. As a surrogate for CD8 T-cell activation in the lungs of virally challenged mice, we measured granzyme B levels in activated CD44HI CD8 T cells, and PMAI-induced IFN-gamma/IL-17a production. The percentages of granzyme B+ve, IFN-gamma-producing, or IL-17a-producing CD8 T cells were not significantly different in the lungs of PR8 NP- and MNP-vaccinated mice (Fig. S3). Thus, differences in CD8 T-cell recall responses did not account for improved IAV-CA04 viral control in the lungs of MNP-vaccinated mice. In contrast to CD8 T cells, we readily detected cytokine-producing CD4 T cells reactive to peptide pool (PP) 7 and PP11, covering the regions 263-277 and 417-431, respectively (Fig. 5B; Fig. S2A). No response was observed in either group for PP2 that corresponded to the predicted 75-89 region. It is noteworthy that both PR8 NP and MNP elicited comparable responses to PP7, but only MNP-induced CD4 T cells that were reactive to PP11. Unlike the response to the vaccine-specific NP311 epitope following the IAV-CA04 challenge, the proportion of polyfunctional (multi-cytokine-producing) CD4 T cells cross-reactive to CA04 NP remained stable even 5 months post-vaccination (Fig. 5C).
