Introduction

With human activities becoming increasingly close to the ocean, emergency response to sudden trauma related to seawater is receiving more and more attention. Unlike on land, due to the diverse types of bacteria, high permeability, and low temperature in seawater, wounds immersed in seawater can be accompanied by severe edema, infection, and pain. More importantly, wounds suffer seawater immersion often result in alkaline pH. The healing ability of wounds soaked in seawater significantly deteriorates, greatly increasing the risk of chronic wound formation. Therefore, timely sealing of wounds, inhibiting bacteria, relieving low-temperature damage and correcting excessive alkaline environments are crucial for later wound healing.

Given that sutures, staples and clips cannot be effectively applied outside the hospital, bioadhesives have been extensively studied for their ease of use and versatility as an alternative to sutures and staples. They can form covalent bonding or non-covalent attractions to tissue surfaces to realize wound closure and provide physical barriers. In addition, more and more additional functions have been assigned to bioadhesives, such as antibacterial and anti-inflammatory functions. alpha-Lipoic acid (LA) is a small molecule coenzyme necessary for the aerobic metabolism of mitochondria, which can eliminate superoxide and peroxide free radicals and has been applied in clinics. Oxidation, heat, light, and mercaptan can trigger disulfide bond cleavage and exchange reactions in the dithiolane to initiate the ring-opening polymerization reaction to prepare poly(lipoic acid) (PLA), which has been reported to possess reliable adhesion, as well as antibacterial and anti-inflammatory performance. However, preparation of PLA-based adhesives cannot be carried out in a mild environment, which usually requires long reaction duration, and special reaction conditions such as high temperature, acid catalysis, solvent displacement, etc. In addition, the as-polymerized PLA-based supramolecular polymers are metastable due to the inverse ring-closing de-polymerization. Additional components such as multiple double-bond monomers, metal ions, ionic liquids, chlorinated organic solvent, dopamine, etc. have to be included. Therefore, developing new method for rapid preparation of LA-derived bioadhesives at room temperature may be more environmentally friendly and convenient.

Moreover, the pH value in the traumatic environment plays a crucial role in the cellular and cell cycle processes during wound healing. The pH of the seawater-immersed wound is usually near 8. When the pH value of the wound is too alkaline, it can cause oxidative stress, which can lead to cell damage (including DNA, protein, and lipid damage) and decreased cell viability, slowing down the healing process. At the same time, the alkaline pH value not only interfere with the production of growth factors and cytokines but also reduce the activity of enzymes and proteins involved in the wound healing process. It has been proven that alkaline environments can reduce the activity of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), which can slow down the proliferation and remodeling stages of wound healing. Besides, the alkaline pH value also increases the risk of wound infection. A high pH value can also reduce the activity of antibiotics, making it easier for pathogens to form infections. It has been reported to fabricate dressings that can intelligently regulate the pH of the wound surface for the healing process. Through material design, the dressings can release and absorb hydrogen ion (H+) separately at different stages of healing in response to the evolution of wound microenvironment, affecting the proliferation and migration of cell on the wound and the activity of various biological factors in the wound, facilitating the physiological processes and accelerating healing of chronic wound. Although studies have presented effective strategies in designing wound healing materials for chronic wound management, there are relatively few reports on the designing of dressings for trauma emergency to intervene in alkaline wounds.

In response to the above issues, there is a need to develop a simple method to rapidly fabricate a stable bioadhesive based on LA at room temperature with the ability of underwater adhesion and neutralizing the alkaline microenvironment of wounds immersed in seawater. The present study developed a kind of bioadhesive based on the supramolecular interactions-driven aggregation of MXene, Ag+ and LA through simple sequential mixing. Molecules could quickly form adhesives in mild environments with underwater and wet adhesion properties. They further co-interacted with tough poly(2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate) (pHEMA) electrospun film to achieve an adhesive tape with stronger adhesion strength. This kind of bioadhesives integrated antibacterial, anti-inflammatory, and photothermal functions. Especially, the non-protonated LA endowed the system with pH responsiveness, intelligently adjusting adverse alkaline environments and providing a favorable microenvironment for wound healing after seawater immersion (Fig. 1; Table 1).

Materials and methods
Materials

LA, silver nitrate (AgNO3), and lithium fluoride (LiF) were purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Technology Co., Ltd. Sodium hydroxide (NaOH), hydrochloric acid (HCl) and poly(2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate) (pHEMA, Mw=10,00,000) were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd.
Preparation of MXene suspension

According to the method described in the literature, Ti3C2Tx was synthesized by removing Al from Ti3AlC2 phase using LiF/HCl etching method. LiF (2.0 g) was slowly dissolved in 40 mL of 9 M hydrochloric acid, followed by the addition of Ti3AlC2 (1 g) to react at 40   C for 24 h. Excess LiF was removed by washing with dilute hydrochloric acid (1 M), followed by being washed with deionized water and centrifuged at a speed of 3500 r/min for 6 times with 5 min each time until the pH was greater than 6. The precipitate was collected, resuspend in 100 mL of water, and sonicated for 2 h in an atmosphere protected by argon gas. Finally, the precipitate was collected after being centrifuged at 3500 r/min for 30 min, and freeze-dried to obtain MXene (Ti3C2Tx) nanosheets. Ti3C2Tx (40 mg) was dispersed into 4 mL of deionized water and stirred for 5 min to obtain an aqueous MXene suspension (10 mg/mL).
Preparation of MAL adhesive

At room temperature, AgNO3 was added to 1 mL of deionized water to prepare a AgNO3 solution with the concentration of 5% w/v. MXene suspension (10 mg/mL) was added to the AgNO3 solution, followed by the addition of LA powder. After mixing and stirring, a black bulk gel was achieved, which was named as "MAL". The effect of adjusting the content of MXene and LA on the performance of MALs was studied. The feeding situation was shown in Table 2.

passages.text: Simulation calculation of MAL formation

Molecular dynamics simulations (MD) were conducted using the Forcite module of Materials Studio 2020 software to investigate the interaction and distribution of LA on MXene surfaces that modified with -F, -OH, and = O in AgNO3 aqueous environments. Of note, based on experimental results and theoretical analysis, Ag+ would be reduced to Ag attached to the surface of MXene, which hads also been taken into account during MD. All molecular dynamics simulations used COMPASS III force field parameters, and the charge of each atom was automatically allocated by the force field. Atom based and Ewald methods were selected to consider the van der Waals and Coulomb interactions, with a cutoff radius of 12.5 angstroms. The MD time step was 1 femtosecond. After constructing the solid (MXene)-liquid interface model, the structure was optimized, and then the Nose thermostat was used to perform NVT simulations at 5000 ps under periodic boundary conditions. During the MD simulation process, a frame trajectory was output every 5 ps. The MD details: the AgNO3 aqueous solution containing LA molecules on the MXene surface was composed of 11 AgNO3, 82 LA, and 409 H2O molecules. The theoretical calculated solution density was 1.186 g/cm3, and the water molecules were modeled using the TIP3P model; For MXene substrate, the transverse x/y dimension was 36.80 x 31.87 A 2, and its upper and lower surfaces were simultaneously modified with -F, -OH, and = O. The relative modification ratios of Ti atoms on the surface are 54.9%, 21.5%, and 23.6%. Before adding the solution, two Ag clusters with dimensions of 8.14 A x 8.14 A x 4.07 A were pre-placed on its surface. After constructing the solid-liquid interface model, the system was minimized in energy and then subjected to a 5 ns NVT simulation.

At the same time, the weak interaction between Ag+ and LA was analyzed using Multiwfn software based on the IGMH method, and the calculation of electrostatic potential was also carried out using Multiwfn software. The plotting was done using software VMD. The Gibbs free energy of carboxyl oxygen with Ag+ and the Gibbs free energy of sulfur adsorption with Ag+ were studied based on density functional theory (DFT). All calculations were performed using the ORCA (version 5.0.3) program for configuration optimization and vibration analysis at the B3LYP-D3 and def2-TZVP basis set levels, while single point energy calculations were performed using the more accurate wB97M-V functional at the def2-TZVPP level. The Gibbs free energy of a compound was equal to the sum of the electronic energy obtained from single point energy calculation and the thermal free energy correction obtained from calculation frequency. The change in Gibbs free energy of a reaction is the difference in Gibbs free energy between the product and the reactant. The binding energy of a compound was calculated by the following formula.
GLA-Ag was the single point energy of the complex formed by LA and Ag+, while GLA and GAg were the single point energies of the compound LA and Ag+, respectively.
Bursting pressure test

Gelatin solution (5% (w/v)) was prepared and applied evenly to the rubber tube that connected to the syringe. After air drying at room temperature, a hole with the diameter of 1 cm was created in the position where was coated with gelatin. Then, MAL was adhered to cover the hole for 5 min for the measurement of the burst pressure. The peak pressure before pressure loss was considered as the burst pressure. All measurements were repeated three times.
Rheological test

MALs with a diameter of 12 mm and a thickness of 5 mm were transferred to a rheometer and fixed using a 12 mm flat fixture to test the relationship between their storage modulus/loss modulus. The testing temperature was 25  C, the frequency scanning range was 0.1-100 Hz, and the strain was 1%.
Evaluation of Photothermal Conversion performance

In order to study the photothermal conversion performance of MAL adhesives, a 808 nm (4 w/cm2) near-infrared laser was used to continuously irradiate MALs with different MXene contents (0% wt, 10% wt, 20% wt, 30% wt) for 100 s. The local temperature and thermal image changes of MALs adhesive were monitored and recorded every 10 s using infrared thermal imaging (Fotrics).
LA release

MALs with same weight were immersed in 10 mL of aqueous solutions with pH 7 and 8, and shaken at a rate of 60 rad/min at 37  C. The UV absorption intensity of the supernatant at 330 nm at a set time point was monitored. The release amount of MALs was calculated based on the standard concentration curve of LA. All tests were repeated three times.
Preparation of adhesive MAL-P tape

pHEMA and LA were dissolved in 70% (v/v) aqueous ethanol, followed by the addition of MXene suspension (10 mg/mL) to form an electrospinning solution with the pHEMA concentration of 13% (w/v), the LA concentration of 30% (w/v) and the MXene content of 3 mg/mL. An electrospinning process was used to generate fibers on an electrospinning equipment (TEADFS-100, Beijing Xinrui Baina Technology Co., Ltd). The electrospinning solution was loaded in 2 mL syringes with a blunt stainless steel 21G needle connected to the positive terminal of high voltage DC supply. The distance between the needle tip and the grounded collector was 15 cm. A 25 kV high DC voltage was then applied between the needle and the collector to initiate the jet. The flow rate was set as 10 microL/min. After the formation of films, they were collected and immersed in AgNO3 solution (50 mg/mL) for 10 min. Then, the films were freeze at -80 oC for 6 h followed by vacuum drying to prepare MAL-P tape.
10 adhesion strength evaluated by lap-shear test

A piece of porcine skin (10 cm x 1 cm) was applied with MAL adhesive with an area of 7.5 cm x 1 cm, then covered with another piece of porcine skin. Then, the electronic universal testing machine (Instron-5943) was used to stretch at a rate of 50 mm/min. The relationship between the force value and displacement feedback from the machine was recorded. At the same time, the surface of two glass slides was coated with 5% (w/v) gelatin solution with a coating size of 2.5 cm x 2.5 cm after air drying for use. MAL adhesive, MAL-P tape with the area of 2.5 cm x 1.0 cm were adhered between the two gelatin-coated glasses. The electronic universal testing machine was used to stretch at a rate of 50 mm/min. 12 in vitro biocompatibility evaluation

The toxicity of MALs and MAL-P tape was evaluated via Cell Counting Kit 8 (CCK8). L929 cells were seeded in 96-well plates and incubated with the extracts from MALs and MAL-P tape for 2 h. Then, 10 microL of CCK-8 reagents were added per well and incubated for another 4 h. The absorbance was measured at wave length of 450 nm using a Microplate Reader (Multiskan GO, USA) to evaluate the cell viability. Similarly, L929 cells were seeded in 96-well plates and incubated with the extracts from MAL-P tape for 1, 3, 5 and 7 days. Then, 10 microL of CCK-8 reagents were added per well and incubated for another 4 h. The absorbance was measured at wave length of 450 nm using a Microplate Reader (Multiskan GO, USA) to evaluate the cell proliferation.

15 seawater-immersed wound healing in vivo

All the animal care, housing, and study procedures for rats complied with the ARRIVE guidelines, and were performed in accordance with the National Research Council's Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. The animal experiment was approved by The First Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang University Ethics Committee (2024 - 1204). SD rats (male) were anesthetized by isoflurane gas, shaved and washed with betadine.

Three incisions with a length of 2 cm were created on the back of each rat, followed by being immersed in seawater that collected from the Huanghai Sea (Qingdao, Shandong Province) for 60 min, which was used as the animal model and employed as the Blank group. For the MAL group, rats with incisions immersed in seawater for 30 min were treated with MAL, followed continuous immersion in seawater for 30 min. For the FibrinGlue group, rats with incisions immersed in seawater for 30 min were treated with FibrinGlue, followed continuous immersion in seawater for 30 min. Rats were sacrificed on day 3, 7 and 14 for skin tissue collection. The middle parts of the scar section were subject to H&E and Masson staining, as well as CD31 & alpha-SMA immunohistochemical staining. Immunofluorescence staining was performed on samples on day 3 to detect the expression of TNF-alpha and TGF-beta, as well as iNOS and CD206. Fluorescence images were analyzed by Image J. A total of 15 rats were used.
16 statistical analysis

Each measurement reported was based on a duplicate analysis of at least three independent experiments. The quantitative results were presented as mean +- SD. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to reveal statistical differences, and p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
Results and discussion
Preparation of MAL adhesive by sequential mixing

For adhesive preparation, there only needed two steps of mixing to achieve rapid preparation of adhesives. The first step was to mix MXene (Ti3C2Tx) suspension with AgNO3 solution. MXene is a type of two-dimensional nanomaterial that has attracted increasing attention in the biomedical field, including antibacterial, biosensing, drug delivery, and disease diagnosis and treatment. The main components of MXene are C, N, O, H, and transition metals. Its surface contains abundant hydrophilic functional groups such as -OH, -F, =O, possessing hydrophilicity and a negatively charged zeta potential, which can stably disperse in water. After this step of mixing, Ag+ could adsorb onto the negatively charged surface of MXene through electrostatic interaction. By receiving electrons from MXene, an oxidation-reduction reaction occurred, leading to the deposition of Ag nanoparticles on MXene nanosheets (Fig. 2A). Figure 2B showed a clear presence of Ag element on MXene-Ag nanosheets. However, according to the Ag+ titration results, not all Ag+ would transform into Ag nanoparticles (TableS1). At the same time, after the first mixing, zeta potential of the nanosheets changed from negative charge to positive charge (Fig. 2C). The second step was to mix the MXene-Ag suspension with LA powder. After this step of mixing, a bulk gel that was named as "MAL" formed immediately, which significantly separated with water (Fig. 2D). This bulk gel was like gum, having a certain cohesive force, and could undergo large deformation without breaking under the action of tensile force (Fig. 2E). The XPS test results showed that after mixing with Ag+, the characteristic peaks of Ti, O, and F elements that could be detected on the surface of MXene were significantly reduced. The characteristic peaks of Ag element all appeared, indicating that Ag appeared on the surface of MXene. After further mixing with LA powder, the characteristic peaks of Ti and F elements almost disappeared. The characteristic peak of Ag element also significantly decreased. At the same time, the characteristic peak of the S element appeared. The characteristic peaks of O and C elements were significantly enhanced. The changes in these characteristic peaks indicated that LA further shielded MXene/Ag (Fig. 2F). FT-IR spectra in Figure S1 showed that a series of characteristic peaks corresponding to the carboxyl groups of LA shifted in MAL, confirming the existence of interactions between the components.

In summary, a bulk gel could be obtained through the above simple two-step mixing. The process was simple and fast. It was worth noting that the three participants in the mixing, MXene suspension, AgNO3 solution, and LA powder, must be mixed in this order. The target gel would not be obtained by other mixing sequences. Since LA powder cannot be dissolved in water, it could only enter the system to form bulk gel through interaction with other components. Whether mixing Ag+ solution with LA powder first or mixing MXene suspension with LA powder first, the supramolecular interaction between them would prevent it from achieving uniform composite with the third component.

Further research was conducted through molecular dynamics simulations to reveal the molecular details of the formation of MAL. As shown in Fig. 3A, B,C, D, based on the component ratio of MAL preparation, a solid-liquid interface model was constructed to minimize energy in the system. After the simulation starts, aggregation were basically completed after 2 ns, with the potential energy, non-bonding energy and total energy of the system tend to stabilize (Fig. 3D). 2 ns ~ 5 ns was only a minor adjustment of the structure. During the simulation process, if the changes in the dithiolane containing disulfide bonds (bright yellow) were focused, it could be observed that the bright yellow disulfide bonds quickly aggregated and approached the Ag nanoparticles. In the 5 ns time graph (Fig. 3B), it could be clearly seen that LA molecules mainly gathered around the Ag nano-clusters, forming interface binding with MXene, but separated from most water molecules, which also confirmed the phenomenon of phase separation between MAL and water after the two-step mixing. As shown in Fig. 3C, there are hydrophobic aggregation of dithiolane, hydrogen bonding between the carboxyl group of LA and the polar groups on the surface of the MXene, and coordination between the disulfide bond of LA and Ag atoms. In addition, by calculating the electrostatic potential of LA and Ag+ in the system (Fig. 3E), it was found that both carboxyl oxygen and disulfide in LA and have significant interaction with Ag+. In addition, density functional theory (DFT) was used to study and calculate the Gibbs free energy of oxygen and sulfur atoms in LA for adsorbing Ag+. The results also showed that Ag could form weak interactions with the carboxyl and disulfide bonds of LA. Moreover, the Gibbs free energy of Ag binding to sulfur atoms was lower, indicating a greater trend in their interaction (FigureS1 Table S2).

There have been reports on the preparation of adhesives based on MXene, LA, and their combination. Their adhesive performance is almost entirely derived from LA. Compared with the adhesives derived from ring opening polymerization of LA, the preparation of MAL gel based on supramolecular interaction did not require high-temperature operations or auxiliary equipment. In addition, the aggregation of small molecules (LA and Ag+) has the characteristic of fast speed. Therefore, simple and rapid preparation was one of the advantages of the present method. Of note, this supramolecular interactions-driven aggregation also accompanied by ring opening polymerization of LA. The supramolecular interactions that lead to the formation of adhesives include hydrophobic aggregation of dithiolane, and this high concentration will cause exchange reactions of disulfide bonds. This could be confirmed by the spectral line changes at 250-300 nm in the UV spectrum (Figure S2). At the same time, characteristic peak at 334 nm that belongs to dithiolane of LA was also presented, indicating that there were still LA monomer.
Adhesion ability of MAL

The adhesion ability of MAL was evaluated. As shown in Fig. 4A, MAL possessed strong adhesion to different substrates, including glass, plastic, and metal (100 g). At the same time, it could tightly adhere to tissues, including liver, kidney, and intestine of chicken. It could also firmly adhere the two separated porcine skins, forming reliable interface adhesion. As shown in Figure S3, under external forces, the failure of adhesion was due to the failure of the MAL body rather than the failure of the bonding interface, confirming that MAL had strong interface adhesion ability.

On the one hand, the lap-shear test on glass coated with gelatin showed that the adhesion strength of MALs increased with the increase of MXene content (Fig. 4B, C). The adhesion strength of M10AL, M20AL and M30AL was 18.9 KPa, 22.3 KPa and 29.5 KPa, respectively. As shown in Figure S4, the adhesion strength of MALs was significantly higher than that of M0AL (adhesive gel without MXene), indicating that the introduction of MXene significantly improved the adhesion performance of MAL. Because the adhesive strength is contributed by both cohesive force and interfacial adhesive force, the presence of MXene significantly improved the storage modulus, thus enhancing the cohesive force and the adhesion strength. According to Fig. 4D and Figure S5, the rheological test results show that the presence of MXene significantly improved the storage modulus of the gel, which might also contribute to the promotion of cohesive force and the adhesion strength. The results of the rubber tube sealing experiment also confirmed that due to the strong interfacial adhesion of MALs and the cohesive force brought by MXene, they could withstand burst pressures higher than 40 KPa. On the other hand, the lap-shear test showed that the adhesion strength of MALs also increased with the increase of LA content (Fig. 4F, G). The adhesion strength of MAL10, MAL20 and MAL30 was 16.4 KPa, 19.4 KPa and 32.5 KPa, respectively. MAL30 was used for the following studies.

Besides, it was found that MAL showed self-reinforcing property. As shown in Fig. 4H, I,J, the adhesion strength of MAL significantly enhanced with duration, while ensuring no significant loss of moisture. After one week and one month, the adhesion strength increased to 68.4 KPa and 90.7 KPa, respectively. The improvement of the adhesion strength might be related to the enhancement of the cohesive force of MAL. As shown in Figure S6, the storage modulus significantly increased after one week. At the same time, with the increase of cohesive force, MAL became increasingly hydrophobic. It was speculated that this might be related to the continuously formed interaction between Ag+/Ag and disulfide bonds, as well as the associated LA polymerization, both of which could significantly enhance the cohesive force of MAL.

For adhesives prepared by LA polymerization, the polymerized LA cannot remain stable and would de-polymerize into oligomers at room temperature, which significantly affect the adhesion strength of the adhesives. Differently, because MAL was mainly formed through non-covalent interaction, although concentration triggered polymerization might also exist in the system, there was no issue of adhesion failure caused by depolymerization. The adhesive prepared by this method exhibited mechanical self-enhancement in long-term observation after preparation, which indicated another advantage of the present method.
Underwater adhesion of MAL

The underwater adhesion characteristics of adhesives and their stable adhesion in wet environments are crucial in emergency treatment of seawater-immersed wounds. As shown in Fig. 5A and Figure S7, MAL could achieve immediate sealing of damaged bottles with seawater flowing or directly stick 100 g weight in the presence of seawater. At the same time, MAL exhibited relatively stable wet adhesion characteristics. As shown in Fig. 5B, the two weights and the two porcine skins bonded by MAL remained stable after being immersed in seawater for 12 h. Normally, the adhesion ability of PLA was believed to originate from carboxyl groups that could form supramolecular interaction with tissues. The adhesion of MAL formed was also derived from carboxyl groups. Meanwhile, due to the dynamic nature of disulfide bonds in MAL, they might also contribute to adhesion by bonding with thiol groups in tissues. Due to the retention of hydrophobic dithiolane and un-deprotonated carboxyl groups during the aggragation process of MAL, it exhibited water repellent properties, enabling them to achieve underwater adhesion while maintaining adhesion stability in wet conditions.

Of note, solvent-free LA melt polymerization can indeed obtain high-performance adhesives. However, the solvent-free LA-derived adhesive required to combine LA powder with the substrate before polymerization and then heated and polymerized to achieve adhesion. If solvent-free PLA was prepared by melt polymerization first and then combined with the substrate, it possessed no adhesion ability. Therefore, although the solvent-free LA-derived adhesive could resist the damage of water to the adhesion strength, it was difficult to achieve instant adhesion underwater. At the same time, as a control, LA dissolved in Tris-base solution was underwent heating at 70 oC for 6 h to yield a PLA-hydrogel adhesive, which was like a pasty maltose, unable to be shaped into a specific form, and quickly swelled and eventually dissolved in water when it was immersed in water (Figure S8). Without the assistance of other components, the adhesion of PLA-based hydrogel adhesives prepared by the polymerization of dissolved LA in water was vulnerable to water damage, and could not realize underwater adhesion. Because LA is insoluble in water and usually requires Tris-base or KOH to deprotonate to achieve dissolution. After deprotonation, -COO- is easy to combine with water molecules, which would destroy its adhesion to substances. Therefore, the adhesion of PLA hydrogel was easy to fail in water.

Of note, because the preparation of MAL was carried out under neutral conditions, the carboxyl groups in LA molecules in MAL were un-deprotonated, which was confirmed by FT-IR in Fig. 5C. The absorption peak near 1700 cm- 1 was the characteristic absorption peak of un-deprotonated carboxyl groups (The characteristic peak of deprotonated carboxyl groups should shift to ~ 1560 cm- 1). However, the carboxyl group of LA is affected by the pH value. Carboxyl groups will undergo deprotonation in alkaline environments. This simple change might have an impact on the performance of MAL. On the one hand, as shown in Figure S9, MAL was stable when being immersed in an acidic hydrochloric acid solution. However, as shown in Fig. 5D, in alkaline environments, especially strong alkaline environments, LA might undergo deprotonation, leading to the failure of MAL. Although MAL disaggregated in aqueous solution with a pH of 10, it was stable in seawater and aqueous solution with a pH of 8 and seawater. Because the pH of wounds immersed in surface seawater is about 8, this study focused on the performance changes of MAL in an environment with a pH of 8. As shown in Fig. 5E, through monitoring, it was found that the release rate and the release amount of LA were significantly higher in an environment with a pH of 8 than in a neutral environment. Of note, the pH neutralization caused by LA release would significantly slow down the release rate of LA, which revealed that MAL was an intelligent adhesive that could release LA in a matching manner by sensing the degree of alkaline environment. Besides, due to the fact that MAL was mainly formed through supramolecular interactions. Ethanol can dissolve LA, leading to the disaggregation of MAL. Therefore, MAL could be easily removed using an ethanol solution (Figure S9). With the release of LA, the adhesion performance of MAL was affected. As shown in Fig. 5F, G, the lap-shear tests results on porcine skin showed that when immersed in seawater with a pH of about 8 for 1 h, the adhesive strength decreased by ~ 30%, which was related to the release of LA in alkaline seawater. However, after immersing for 24 h, the adhesive strength significantly increased, which might be the result of the synergistic effect of reduced release of LA after pH neutrality and self-reinforcement of MAL.

In the design of MALs, LA played a role in both pH intervention and adhesion. Therefore, while adjusting pH through deprotonation of LA, it would negatively affect adhesion. However, the pH of shallow seawater is weakly alkaline. The research data showed that MAL was stable in seawater and alkaline solutions with a pH of 8. Only a strongly alkaline environment could significantly disrupt the interactions between components, leading to the disintegration of MAL. The response of MAL to pH was specifically the response to alkaline environments. After the pH of the wound returns to neutral, the release of LA in MAL would significantly decrease. Therefore, MAL would not rapidly disintegrate to lose tissue adhesion in weakly alkaline environments. In addition, its self-reinforcing properties would compensate for this loss of adhesion over a longer period of application time.
MAL integrated with pHEMA electrospun film for preparation of strong adhesive tape

Although MAL exhibited reliable tissue adhesion, due to its non-covalent interactions between molecules, its interfacial adhesion was strong but cohesive was low, which made it difficult to achieve greater breakthroughs in adhesion strength. Therefore, considering the complexity of chemical modification, this study proposed to integrate MAL with polymer film, providing high cohesion through the polymer film while retaining MAL's strong interfacial adhesion to synergistically improve the adhesive strength.

Adhesion of MAL-P tape. (A) Process of MAL-P tape production. (B) SEM images and EDS scanning of S and Ti elements. (C) Tensile test of MAL-P tape. (D) Tensile modulus of MAL-P tape (*p < 0.05). (E) Images to show the strong adhesion of MAL-P tape. (F) Lap-shear test of MAL-P tape. (G) Adhesion strength of MAL-P tape (*p < 0.05)

The integration process was not simply about sticking the polymer film and MAL together but rather combining the preparation process of MAL with the preparation process of the polymer film, allowing MXene/Ag+/LA to interact through supramolecular interactions while also achieving stable binding with the polymer film matrix. Therefore, pHEMA, which is rich in hydrogen bonding is selected as the matrix for polymer film. The film was prepared by electrospinning pHEMA aqueous ethanol solution containing MXene and LA, followed by immersion in Ag+ solution to obtain adhesive tape, which was further strengthened by freeze-drying (Fig. 6A). As shown in Fig. 6B, the pHEMA/MXene/LA film obtained by electrospinning had a distinct fiber stacking structure, with fiber diameters of approximately 1000-2000 nm. The EDS scan results showed the distribution of S and Ti elements in the film matrix, confirming that LA and MXene were dispersed in the pHEMA fiber matrix. After soaking in Ag+ solution, Ag+ interact with MXene and LA in the matrix, causing damage to the fiber structure and significant fusion between fibers. However, the film still maintained a porous structure, which was beneficial for increasing the contact area with the tissue and thus improving the adhesion strength.

Accordingly, post-processing such as freeze-drying or heating can significantly improve the stability of pHEMA electrospun films. Because heating can cause LA polymerization, this study post-treated the film through freeze-drying to obtain the final adhesive tape, MAL-P tape. As shown in Fig. 6C, D, the tensile strength of the film after freeze-drying treatment was significantly improved, and its tensile modulus was increased by about 10 times. As the cohesion of the tape increased, the tape exhibited significantly improved adhesion. As shown in the Fig. 6E, in addition to being able to tightly adhere tissues, a square MAL-P tape with a side length of about 9.5 mm could firmly adhere two gelatin-coated glass slides and carried a 3 kg weight. The lap-shear test results showed that even without freeze-drying post-treatment, the adhesive strength of the tape had been significantly improved, reaching ~ 0.6 MPa. The adhesive tape treated by freeze-drying had an adhesion strength exceeding 2 MPa due to improved cohesion (Fig. 6F, G). Without freeze-drying, the adhesion strength of MAL-P tape was significantly improved compared to MAL, revealing that the increased cohesion brought by the composite of PHEMA film contributed to the improvement of adhesion strength. The reason for the further enhancement of adhesive strength of the MAL-P tape after post-processing was also due to the further increase in cohesive force caused by freeze-drying. Similar to polyvinyl alcohol, the freeze-thaw process could promote the formation of hydrogen bonds in the hydroxyl groups, thereby increasing the physical crosslinking density and affecting the various physical and chemical properties of the material. In MAL-P tape, the formation of hydrogen bonds including that formed by hydroxyl groups in PHEMA and those formed between components including LA, MXene, and PHEMA was promoted during the freeze-drying process, leading to a significant increase in intermolecular forces and a tighter bond between fibers. Therefore, the mechanical properties of PHEMA membranes combined with MAL were significantly enhanced. The regulation of different adhesion strengths could be applicable to different application requirements.
In vitro evaluation of MALs and MAL-P tape

The biocompatibility results of MALs with different components and MAL-P tape showed that they did not exhibit cytotoxicity at different component concentrations (Fig. 7A). Cells co-cultured with MAL-P tape did not show significant apoptosis within 7 days (Fig. 7B, C). Besides, the results of in vitro antibacterial experiments showed that MAL-P tape exhibited significant antibacterial functions to both S. aureus and P. aeruginosa (Fig. 7D, E). Accordingly, MXene, Ag+ and LA were all reported to possess antibacterial ability. Compared with the control group, the presence of MAL-P could reduce the bacterial survival rate to below ~ 12%.

passages.text: In addition, the MAL-P tape integrated with MXene, LA and Ag+ had multiple biological functions. The release of LA had positive effects on seawater-immersed wounds. For one thing, in alkaline environment, the release of LA was closely related to its deprotonation, which would significantly affect the pH of the alkaline environment. As shown in Fig. 7F, the pH value of the alkaline aqueous solution significantly reduced to neutral after the immersion of MAL-P tape. At the same time, the alkaline skin wound of rat immersed in seawater was adjusted to neutral after the application of MAL-P tape for 1 h. The pH value in the traumatic environment plays a crucial role in the cellular and cell cycle processes during wound healing. A healthy wound environment typically has a pH value between 6 and 7, which helps to control the growth of harmful bacteria and prevent infection. Such pH responsive design and intervention of alkaline wound function have not been reported in previous LA-based adhesives. For another, due to the antioxidant function of LA, the released LA could significantly clear DPPH. As shown in Fig. 7G, H, after 48 h, the activity of DPPH remains less than 5%.

Taken together, in a weakly alkaline wet environment such as seawater-immersed wound, MAL-P tape could not only stably adhere to the wound, but also intervene in alkaline wounds by releasing H+, adjusting the wound pH to neutral. The released LA exhibited strong ROS-scavenging ability. MAL-P tape also exhibited significant antibacterial activity. Besides, gas permeability rate (GPR) testing showed MAL-P tape had better air permeability than MAL, indicating it had both waterproof and a certain degree of breathability (Figure S10). Its breathability might be related to the porous skeleton composed of PHEMA fibers. Based on these unique properties, further research was conducted to evaluate the treatment effect of MAL-P tape on seawater-immersed wounds through animal evaluation.

Intervention of MAL-P tape in alkaline wound

The rat skin incision model immersed in seawater was used to evaluate the function of MAL-P tape. Considering that MAL-P tape's ability to achieve underwater adhesion and intelligently intervene in alkaline microenvironments, the modified animal model by applying MAL-P tape to the wound after soaking in seawater and continuing to soak it in seawater for a period of time was created to verify the reliability of MAL-P's wet adhesion and ability to adjust pH. Realistic representation of wound cares such as cleaning with a neutral or weak acid solution prior to closure were not carried out. This is also simulating the process of continuing to wait for rescue after treating the wound on one's own. As shown in Fig. 8A, B, after seawater immersion, the wound healing function was significantly inhibited. After 14 days of monitoring, it was found that the wound had not yet fully healed with the presence of the scab in the Blank group. This might be related to the alkalinity and infection of wounds caused by seawater immersion. In the FibrinGlue group, the application of FibrinGlue had played a certain positive role. Timely sealing of the wound was beneficial for protecting the wound, thus facilitating the healing of the wound in the later stage. At day 14, the area of unhealed wounds was smaller than that of the Blank group. However, since FibrinGlue was not suitable for adhesion in wet environments and had poor adhesion stability in seawater, it could still be observed that the wound was not completely closed after 14 days. The best healing outcome was the wound treated by the MAL-P tape in the MAL-P tape group. The wound healing was significantly enhanced at day 7. The area of unhealed wounds in the MAL-P tape group was significantly smaller than that of the other groups. Although the traces of the wound could still be observed at day 14, the skin had completely closed. Of note, in the present animal model, wounds treated by MAL-P tapes were continued to soak in seawater to test the effectiveness of the adhesive in seawater. The results showed that all MAL-P tapes stably adhered on the wound during the seawater immersion duration without any cases of detachment, indicating the reliability of MAL-P tape for wound adhesion in seawater. Besides, MAL-P tape was not replaced throughout the entire repair period. MAL-P tape eventually fell off on its own during the wound healing process (at 7-10 d post-treatment).

Histological staining, including H&E and Masson staining showed that in the Blank group, after seawater immersion, there was significant inflammatory cell infiltration in the wound site (Fig. 8C). The normal skin tissues did not form continuous healing. In the FibrinGlue group, significant neo-tissues were found to fill in the wounds. However, the neo-tissue had poor continuity. The epithelialization was still not complete. On the contrary, the incision treated with MAL-P tape in the MAL-P tape group showed that the skins were well-integrated by the neo-tissue, which possessed continuous and complete epidermal continuity. As shown in Fig. 8D, further CD31 & alpha-SMA immunohistochemical staining showed that during the observation period, wound vascularization was significantly inhibited in the Blank group. Vascularization is an important process in the early stage of wound healing. Once the degree of vascularization is insufficient, the healing of the wound will slow down and develop into a chronic non-healing wound. Although FibrinGlue was used to seal the wound, the vascularization process was delayed due to the poor microenvironment of the wound. In the MAL-P tape group, due to the protection in a wet environment, correction of alkaline microenvironment, antibacterial and anti-inflammatory functions, the benign microenvironment intervened by MAL-P tape made the vascularization ability of wound normal. As shown in Fig. 8D and Figure S11, there was significant vascularization at 7 days, indicating that wound was in the repair stage. As the repair progresses, the degree of wound vascularization decreased after 14 days, indicating that the wound entered the period of vascular inhibition and remodeling. This was a relatively normal process of wound healing.

The inflammatory microenvironment of the early stage of wounds on day 3 was evaluated. Because of the regulation of pH and barrier protection of seawater-immersed wound by MAL-P tape, the wound microenvironment has been positively intervened. As shown in Figure S12, tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) immunofluorescence staining showed that wounds immersed in seawater in the Blank group showed strong inflammatory signal, indicating significant inflammation. Similarly, wounds closed with FibrinGlue also showed extensive expression of TNF-alpha. While wounds closed with MAL-P tape showed the lowest inflammatory signal intensity of TNF-alpha. On the contrary, wounds treated with MAL-P tape exhibited the highest inflammatory signal intensity of transforming growth factor-beta1 (TGF-beta1), indicating the application of MAL promoted the secretion of anti-inflammatory factors and inhibited local inflammatory response to accelerate wound healing.

TGF-beta1 plays an important role in mediating M1/M2 subtype transformation and the subsequent tissue repair and angiogenesis. The up-regulation of TGF-beta1 in the MAL-P tape group promoted angiogenesis. To verify the transformation effect of MAL-P tape on macrophages in vivo, iNOS (M1 type macrophage marker) staining and CD206 (M2 type macrophage marker) immunofluorescence staining were carried out. According to Fig. 8E, F, iNOS expression in the Blank group and the FibrinGlue group was both higher. While in the MAL-P tape group, CD206 expression was higher, indicating that the application of MAL-P tape significantly affected the macrophage polarization, leading to more M2 macrophages, which mainly secrete high levels of anti-inflammatory cytokines and repair growth factors to promote tissue regeneration. Therefore, the pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory factors immunofluorescence staining results, as well as the macrophage marker immunofluorescence staining results illustrated that the application of MAL-P tape provided a positive microenvironment for tissue repair, thereby promoting healing of seawater-immersed wound.

Besides, the presence of MXene endowed MAL-P tape with excellent photothermal conversion function (Figure S13), which might also have a positive impact on trauma emergency treatment in the ocean. Thanks to the advanced photothermal conversion performance of MXene, the photothermal conversion performance of MAL-adhesive was superior. Compared with other nanomaterials with photothermal conversion properties such as Fe3O4 that mixed with Ag+/LA, MAL-adhesives could achieve faster photothermal conversion. Usually, low temperatures in the ocean can seriously affect wound healing. MAL-P tape could efficiently convert light energy into heat energy, which might also be used to alleviate local low temperatures and promote wound healing.
Conclusion

In summary, the present study proposed a simple and rapid method for preparing LA-based adhesives at room temperature. By sequentially mixing MXene, Ag+, and LA, a bioadhesive named MAL was rapidly formed based on the supramolecular interactions-drived aggregation. Furthermore, based on these supramolecular interactions, pHEMA/MXene/LA was subjected to electrospinning, followed by immersing with Ag+ and freeze-drying to yield an electrospun film, MAL-P tape with the strong adhesion strength as high as 2 MPa. The adhesives exhibited reliable underwater adhesion, showing stable adhesion on skin in seawater. In terms of biological activity, adhesives were sensitive to alkaline environments and could adjust the pH of alkaline seawater-immersed wounds to normal pH. At the same time, LA was released into wounds to exert anti-inflammatory functions. In addition, MAL-P tape also exhibited significant antibacterial property. The intervention of wound pH, anti-inflammatory and antibacterial functions enabled MALs to protect wounds, significantly improve the microenvironment of seawater-immersed wounds, promoting wound healing and preventing wounds from developing into chronic wounds.

passages.text: Calciphylaxis: Beating the Odds

Calciphylaxis is an obliterative vasculopathy characterized by ischemic cutaneous necrosis secondary to the calcification of small- and medium-caliber blood vessels. This condition poses a significant therapeutic challenge and is often associated with poor outcomes.

We report the case of a 59-year-old man who had been on renal replacement therapy for 28 years and presented with a painful necrotic ulcer on his left leg, which progressively worsened over three weeks. A skin biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of calciphylaxis. The treatment approach included intensified hemodialysis, optimization of mineral and bone disorder management, treatment of secondary bacterial infection, intravenous sodium thiosulfate infusion, chemical and surgical debridement, and partial-thickness skin grafting. This comprehensive strategy resulted in complete wound healing within three months.

passages.text: This case highlights the importance of early diagnosis and a multidisciplinary approach in managing calciphylaxis, a rare condition associated with a highly unfavorable prognosis.
Introduction

Calciphylaxis, also known as calcific uremic arteriolopathy, is a rare and life-threatening obliterative vasculopathy characterized by ischemic skin necrosis due to the calcification and occlusion of small- and medium-sized blood vessels. This vascular calcification leads to luminal narrowing and thrombosis, resulting in reduced blood flow, tissue ischemia, and subsequent skin necrosis . Although it is most commonly observed in patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) undergoing dialysis, calciphylaxis can also occur in earlier stages of chronic kidney disease (CKD), after kidney transplantation, and, rarely, in individuals with normal kidney function. The condition is associated with a poor prognosis, with a one-year mortality rate reaching up to 80% in patients with CKD.

Numerous risk factors have been associated with calciphylaxis, including disturbances in calcium-phosphate metabolism, obesity, diabetes mellitus, female sex, white race, vitamin K deficiency, and prolonged use of calcium-based phosphate binders or vitamin D supplements. Additionally, patients often present with elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels, hyperphosphatemia, and a deficiency of natural inhibitors of calcification, such as fetuin-A and matrix Gla protein. However, not all affected individuals display these abnormalities, highlighting the multifactorial and poorly understood pathogenesis of this condition.

passages.text: The clinical presentation is typically characterized by painful, ischemic skin lesions that frequently progress to necrosis, increasing the risk of infection and sepsis. Given its dismal prognosis and limited therapeutic options, calciphylaxis underscores the critical need for early recognition and a multidisciplinary approach to treatment .
Case presentation

A 57-year-old male presented to the emergency department with a three-week history of a painful ulcer that appeared spontaneously on the back of his left lower leg and was progressively increasing in size. He denied fever, chills, or any other systemic symptoms.

The patient had a 28-year history of ESRD, managed with two kidney transplants that lasted a total of 11 years, along with 17 years of hemodialysis, including periods between the two transplants and following the second transplant. His medical history was notable for secondary hyperparathyroidism, treated with etelcalcetide (5 mg three times per week) and alfacalcidol (0.5 mcg three times per week), as well as paroxysmal atrial fibrillation managed with long-term anticoagulation using warfarin.

On physical examination, the patient was afebrile, with a blood pressure of 135/77 mmHg and a heart rate of 75 beats per minute. He presented with a necrotic ulcer approximately 4 cm in diameter on the back of his left lower leg (Figure 1). There were no signs of cellulitis or systemic infection at the time of presentation. Cardiopulmonary and abdominal examinations were unremarkable.
Necrotic lesion at admission.
Necrotic ulcer approximately 4 cm in size on the posterior left lower leg, with a central black eschar and an erythematous border, consistent with ischemic necrosis and calciphylaxis.
Laboratory results at admission are summarized in Table 1.

Given the clinical presentation and the patient's history, calciphylaxis was suspected, and the patient was admitted under the care of the nephrology team. A skin biopsy confirmed the diagnosis, revealing vascular calcification and thrombosis in small- and medium-sized arterioles, accompanied by tissue necrosis. Non-calcium-based phosphate binders (sevelamer) were initiated, and the calcimimetic therapy (etelcalcetide) was continued. Hemodialysis was intensified to four sessions per week to optimize metabolic control and fluid balance. Warfarin was replaced with enoxaparin adjusted to renal function, and alfacalcidol was discontinued.

On the fifth day of hospitalization, the patient developed signs of local infection around the ulcer, including erythema, warmth, and swelling. Laboratory tests showed a leukocytosis of 13,600/muL with 10,200 neutrophils/muL and a C-reactive protein (CRP) of 115 mg/L. Empiric antibiotic therapy with vancomycin and meropenem was initiated to target possible Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens. Blood cultures and a swab of the lesion were collected but yielded no microbial growth. Antibiotic therapy was continued for 14 days, leading to the resolution of the inflammatory signs.

Intravenous sodium thiosulfate therapy was started on the seventh day of hospitalization, at a dose of 25 grams three times weekly after dialysis. Early involvement of the Plastic Surgery team facilitated both chemical debridement with silver sulfadiazine and surgical debridement to remove necrotic tissue and promote wound healing. Although the patient was listed for hyperbaric oxygen therapy, the wound began to show significant improvement before this intervention could be initiated.

By the 41st day of hospitalization, a partial-thickness skin graft was harvested from the ipsilateral thigh and successfully applied to the wound bed. The patient continued to demonstrate gradual improvement, achieving complete wound healing and being discharged on the 47th day of hospitalization. At the one-month outpatient follow-up consultation, the lesion was fully healed, with no signs of recurrence or complications (Figure 2).
Calciphylaxis lesion at the one-month follow-up consultation.
Healed lesion on the posterior left lower leg at the one-month follow-up, showing complete wound closure with residual scarring and no evidence of active infection or recurrence.
Discussion

Calciphylaxis, or calcific uremic arteriolopathy, is a rare but life-threatening condition that primarily affects patients with ESRD undergoing dialysis. Despite advancements in understanding the disease, calciphylaxis remains associated with a poor prognosis, with mortality rates reported to range between 50% and 80% within the first year, largely due to complications such as sepsis and delayed wound healing. Furthermore, calciphylaxis carries a significant risk of recurrence, particularly in patients with ongoing inflammation or inadequate control of underlying risk factors, such as hyperparathyroidism and elevated calcium-phosphorus product levels.

This case underscores the importance of identifying risk factors and implementing early interventions in patients at high risk for calciphylaxis. The patient's long-standing ESRD, having been on renal replacement therapy (RRT) for 28 years, coupled with secondary hyperparathyroidism and chronic warfarin use, placed him in a high-risk category. Warfarin is a known contributor to calciphylaxis due to its inhibition of vitamin K-dependent proteins, such as matrix Gla protein, a critical inhibitor of vascular calcification. Its replacement with enoxaparin may have mitigated further progression of vascular calcification. The lower extremities, particularly the legs, are common sites for calciphylaxis lesions due to reduced vascular reserve, ischemic predisposition, and increased susceptibility to chronic microtrauma, all of which exacerbate tissue necrosis in these regions.

Management of calciphylaxis requires a multidisciplinary approach addressing both systemic and local factors contributing to disease progression. Sodium thiosulfate was initiated as part of the therapeutic regimen. Although its precise mechanism of action is not fully understood, sodium thiosulfate is thought to reduce vascular calcification by chelating calcium, enhancing its solubility, and mitigating oxidative stress. It has also been associated with improvements in pain and wound healing in patients with calciphylaxis.

Optimization of mineral and bone metabolism was another cornerstone of this patient's management. Sevelamer was introduced to reduce phosphorus while minimizing further calcium overload. Since the calcium-phosphorus product is one of the main risk factors for the onset and progression of calciphylaxis, it was used even with normal serum phosphorus levels, effectively reducing the product without ever causing hypophosphatemia. Etelcalcetide was continued to address secondary hyperparathyroidism, without raising the phosphate or calcium levels. These interventions are essential in controlling the calcium-phosphate balance and preventing vascular calcification and subsequent tissue necrosis.

Secondary bacterial infection of necrotic ulcers is a common and serious complication of calciphylaxis. In this case, the development of local signs of infection, including erythema, swelling, and elevated inflammatory markers, prompted the timely initiation of broad-spectrum antibiotics. The absence of microbial growth in blood cultures and lesion swabs highlights the challenge of identifying causative organisms in such cases. Nonetheless, early and effective antimicrobial treatment was crucial in resolving the infection and preventing systemic complications.

The involvement of the Plastic Surgery team was decisive in achieving a successful outcome. Early debridement, both chemical and surgical, was essential to create an optimal environment for wound healing. Chemical debridement with silver sulfadiazine not only controlled bacterial colonization but also facilitated autolytic debridement by maintaining a moist wound bed. Surgical debridement further ensured the removal of nonviable tissue. A partial-thickness skin graft, harvested from the ipsilateral thigh, was successfully applied to the prepared wound bed. This intervention accelerated wound closure and minimized the risk of long-term complications such as chronic infection or limb dysfunction. The early collaboration with plastic surgery points to the importance of integrating specialized surgical care into the management of calciphylaxis, particularly for large or refractory wounds.
Conclusions

This case highlights the role of early recognition and a multidisciplinary approach in the management of calciphylaxis, a condition that poses significant therapeutic challenges. A combination of systemic therapy, advanced wound care, and surgical interventions was key to achieving a positive outcome in this patient. Continued research is necessary to enhance treatment protocols and improve survival rates for those affected by this rare but severe disease.

With a treatment plan guided by the latest literature and a close collaboration with the plastic surgery team, complete therapeutic success was achieved. This case underscores the importance of maintaining a high index of suspicion and providing timely interventions for a disease that, although rare, is frequently associated with poor outcomes.
